activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A note one octave higher than another vibrates at exactly twice its frequency, so the A above A440 is 880 hertz.
story:
James had four days to learn the second half of the piece, and the piano in the living room was fighting him the whole way. The audition video for the youth orchestra had to be uploaded by Sunday at midnight, no extensions, and the passage that kept breaking apart was the octave jump in measure thirty-two, where the left hand had to land on the A below middle C while the right hand struck the A above it, together, cleanly, at speed.

He set his phone on the music rack with the tuner app open, the way Makayla had shown him at school. "You're sharp everywhere," she'd said, tapping his practice notebook. "You can't hear it yourself yet, so let the machine tell you." She was coming over Saturday to run the recording, which left him Thursday and Friday alone with the metronome and his own impatience.

The tuner gave him numbers, and numbers felt like something he could trust. He played the low A, held it, and watched the screen settle on 440. Then he played the higher A, the one his right hand kept missing, and the number that bloomed there stopped him with his fingers still on the keys. 880. Exactly double. He played both again, slower, watching. 440, then 880, as if the two notes were the same note extruded into a longer, thinner version of itself, stretched to twice the frequency. He had never thought of octaves as arithmetic before, and now the fact of it sat in his chest, doubled and doubled again.

Ricky, sprawled on the couch with a controller, craned his head around. "Why do you keep playing the same note like forty times?"

"They're not the same note. Look." James played the low A and pointed at the screen. "Four forty. Now watch." He struck the A an octave up. "Eight eighty. One octave higher is exactly twice the frequency." The words came out before he'd decided to say them, and saying them made them real.

"So it's math," Ricky said, and went back to his game, but James kept staring at the screen. If the octave was a clean doubling, then the interval was fixed, objective, the same on every piano in the world. So why did his jump feel different every time?

The answer arrived Friday night, and it wasn't about his hands. He was playing the passage for the camera, testing angles, when the tuner caught something he hadn't noticed. On the third repetition the low A drifted flat, sliding under 440 by a margin that flickered and grew. He played it again, listening hard. The string was sour, a faint beat in the sound, and it had probably been sour for months. Every practice session, every recording he'd made, that A had been wrong, and his ear had quietly accepted it, folding it into an amalgam of everything he thought the piano was supposed to sound like. His teacher had moved away in the spring; nobody had tuned the piano since.

Mr. Traoré from next door was out on his porch in the diaphanous evening light, and James crossed the lawn with his phone still showing the drifting number. "Sir, do you know anyone who tunes pianos? Like, before Sunday."

Mr. Traoré looked at the screen for a long moment. "Before Sunday," he repeated. "You have a recital?"

"An audition. Video. It's due Sunday night." James heard the pitch of his own voice climb and made himself level it. "The A string's gone flat. I just found out tonight."

"My brother tuned them, back home. Me, no." Mr. Traoré rubbed his jaw. "There is a man in Fairview, but Friday he will not answer, and Saturday, I don't know."

James went back inside and played the passage once more, listening for the waver with his new knowledge, and now that he knew, he couldn't unhear it. The wrongness was obvious, glaring, a crack in something he'd trusted. Yet when he played the jump with the sour A, the doubling still held, 440 and 880 in his mind if not under his fingers, and he understood that the idea of the octave was more durable than any one broken string.

Saturday morning Makayla arrived with a tripod and two granola bars, and he told her about the tuner, the numbers, the drift. She sat down at the piano and played the two As herself, frowning.

"So you can't fix it in time," she said.

"I could record the right hand and left hand separately and layer them," James said. "Or I could play the whole thing a half step up, transpose everything, avoid that string entirely. Or I just play it flat and hope they think it's the recording." He looked at the phone on the rack, the tuner still open, the number for the low A hovering a few cents under 440 like a held breath. "Which one is honest?"

Makayla set up the tripod without answering, angling the lens toward the keys, and James sat down and put his hands where they belonged.

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: Research by Gabriele Wulf found that learners usually improve faster when told to focus on the effect of a movement, such as the target, rather than on their own body parts.
story:
Brianna unfolded her notebook on the bleachers and watched the seventh-graders throw the ball everywhere except to each other. Cristian had given her this team the way people give away things they're tired of carrying, with a shrug and the words "they're yours now," and she had said yes because she wanted, more than almost anything, to be trusted with something. Now the whistle hung around her neck, its brass scratched from years of someone else's mouth, her grandfather's patrimony handed over at the kitchen table last month with only one instruction: don't let them run wild.

They ran wild. She spent the first practice shouting corrections that felt like things she'd heard coaches say, bend your wrist, step into it, tuck your elbow, and the passes got worse, not better, as the girls thought their way through their own arms and forgot to look up. One of them, a small obstreperous kid named Ireland who argued with every call, finally sat down on the ball and said, "My brain is full."

That night Brianna lay on her bed with her phone above her face, searching. Her father had shown her how to look things up when she was small, and she still did it his way, plain words, no shortcuts. She found a study by a researcher named Gabriele Wulf, and she read the sentence three times. Learners usually improve faster when they're told to focus on the effect of a movement, like the target, instead of on their own body parts. She read it again, slower, feeling something turn over in her.

She had a flashback then, uninvited, of tenth grade, Ms. Yang's classroom, the afternoon sun flat on the desks. Ms. Yang had said, about essay writing, "Stop watching your own pen. Look at what the sentence is doing to the reader." Brianna had thought it was a figure of speech. She sat up on her bed. Maybe it had never been a figure of speech at all.

At the next practice she taped paper plates to the wall behind the rim, low, where hands would be. "New rule," she said. "Don't think about your arms. Hit the plate." The girls looked at her like she'd cancelled basketball. Ireland stood with the ball on her hip and said, "That's it? That's the drill?" and Brianna said, "That's the whole drill," and the first pass missed by a foot, and the second missed by less, and by the end of the hour the gym sounded different, balls slapping flat against paper, and Ireland was grinning in a way that made Brianna's chest go hot with something close to exhilaration.

But it cost her something, too. Cristian came to watch the last half hour, arms crossed, and afterward he said the drills looked like games a camp counselor would run, no footwork, no fundamentals, and that her grandfather would have hated it. He said "your grandfather" the way people say a name they know will land. Brianna had put the old man's whistle in her mouth every practice, and she didn't know whether he would have hated it or whether he'd been saying bend your wrist for thirty years because nobody had ever told him anything different. Both of those could be true. She couldn't ask him; the kitchen table was emptier now than it had been in the fall.

The girls kept improving. In the fourth practice they hit the plates without aiming, eyes up, calling names, and one pass, Ireland to a girl cutting along the baseline, arrived so cleanly that the girl caught it without looking and laid it in, and the whole gym went quiet for a second before the shouting started. Brianna blew the whistle and it sounded different in her mouth, like a word she finally understood the meaning of, though she couldn't have said what the meaning was.

Cristian stood at the door with his bag over his shoulder, watching. When she walked over, water bottle sweating in her hand, he said, "Fine. It works." He didn't say anything else, and neither did she. Behind him Ireland was taping the plates back up herself, tearing the tape with her teeth, climbing onto the second bleacher to reach the high one, and Brianna watched her stretch the tape tight across the paper, once, twice, until it held.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: The 26th Amendment, which set the US voting age at 18, was ratified in 1971 in about three months, faster than any other amendment.
story:
Christian kept the sample ballot folded in his back pocket all through last period, and by the time Mr. Romano dimmed the lights for the documentary, the paper had gone soft as cloth. The election was Tuesday. He would be voting in his first one, in the gym at the middle school two blocks from his house, and he still had not decided on the school board race, where two candidates he actually knew were running against each other.

"All right," Mr. Romano said when the film ended and the lights came up. "We have ten minutes. Anyone voting Tuesday?" A few hands went up, Christian's among them, and Mr. Romano nodded as though this settled something. "Then you've done something my father couldn't do at your age."

Elena, who sat in front of Christian and turned around whenever the room got interesting, frowned at that. "Couldn't vote at eighteen? Why not?"

"The Twenty-sixth Amendment," Mr. Romano said. "Ratified in 1971. Before that, you had to be twenty-one." He picked up a stack of handouts and started passing them down the rows, which was his way of ending a subject. But he paused at Elena's desk. "Three months, that ratification took. Faster than any other amendment, before or since."

"Three months," Elena repeated, turning partway toward Christian. "Our entire semester project took longer than that."

Christian wrote it on the margin of the handout without quite knowing why. That Sunday his grandfather came for dinner, and Christian, carrying the salad out, mentioned he was voting Tuesday. He expected the usual joke about choosing wisely, but his grandfather set down the serving spoon and said, "You know I couldn't have, at your age. Twenty-one was the rule when I turned eighteen. They changed it in seventy-one." He said it the way he mentioned most things, flatly, as though reporting weather from a town nobody lived in anymore, and Christian, surprised, thought of Mr. Romano saying the same thing in the classroom and felt the two of them linked across a distance he couldn't measure.

"You would have been drafted, though," Christian's mother said from the stove. "At eighteen. You just couldn't vote."

His grandfather didn't answer that. He spooned more rice onto his plate.

Monday after school, Christian sat on the bleachers by the field with Abel, who had turned eighteen in October and had already mailed his ballot. "I voted for Yamada," Abel said, naming one of the school board candidates. "She came to my sister's IEP meeting when nobody else would. Sat there for two hours."

"Ross hired me at the pool," Christian said. "Taught me to run the chlorine tests. He's running too." Abel nodded and didn't argue, which was worse somehow, because it left Christian alone with the fact that he had two debts and one vote. The bleachers were cold through his jeans. Practice ended across the field, and the coach's whistle carried thin in the November air.

He took out the sample ballot and looked at the two names until they stopped being names and became a small square he had to fill in by seven tomorrow night, because the polls closed then and his shift at the pool began at seven thirty. The deadline was ordinary and absolute, which he found almost reassuring. Everything else about the decision kept bending.

That night he read both candidates' statements again, and somewhere in the middle of Yamada's, about class sizes and the transportation budget, he heard Ross's voice saying dilution rates matter more than people think, that a wrong measurement can transmute clean water into something you have to close the pool over. He also heard Elena describing Yamada's two hours at her sister's meeting. One candidate had been good to him in particular; the other had been good to people who had no one else showing up. He tried to weigh these and found his jaundiced suspicion rising, the old one, that both of them were just angling for something, and he had to put that down deliberately, like putting down a phone, because it wasn't evidence, only mood.

He thought about the three months. An entire country had argued its way to eighteen-year-olds and the vote, and done it faster than anyone had ever done anything like it, and still his grandfather's own eighteenth year had come and gone without a ballot in it. Christian had exactly one night. It seemed absurd, the whole apparatus waiting on his pen, and also not absurd at all, because the whole point of the apparatus was that it did wait, that it waited for each person singularly, at a folding table in a middle school gym, however late the right had come to people his age.

In the morning he walked the two blocks in a wind that rattled the chain-link around the school yard. The gym smelled of floor wax and coffee. A woman with a clipboard found his name, a man in a lanyard showed him the booth, and he stood with the pen hovering the way you hover at a pool's edge, aware that the jump would commit him whether or not he felt ready. He filled in the president, the senate, the county judge. Then the school board square, and he thought of Abel and of the chlorine tests and of his grandfather spooning rice in silence, and he marked one of the names, and afterward, stepping out into the lot, he could not have told you which reasons had won, only that he had walked in with the question and was walking out having answered it, the paper folded and gone from his hands into a machine that swallowed it with a small mechanical shrug.

Elena was coming up the sidewalk, her own hands in her pockets. "Did you vote?" she called.

"Ten minutes ago."

"For who, on the school board?"

He shook his head, smiling a little, and held the door of the gym open for her. "You first."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Earthenware pottery is normally fired below about 1,200 degrees Celsius, while porcelain is fired between about 1,200 and 1,400 degrees Celsius.
story:
Riley had until Saturday, and by Friday afternoon he had managed to operationalize that deadline into a list taped above the library's community kiln: trim, sign, dry, fire, cool, carry to the display case by ten in the morning. The kiln lived in the back of the makerspace the city had shoehorned into the library's old periodical room, a squat electric oven behind a folding screen, and Riley had spent every afternoon that week there, building a small covered jar out of clay his grandfather had left in the garage. He thought of it, only half jokingly, as patrimony: forty pounds of grey-green earth in a cracked bin, the last thing connecting him to a man who had died before Riley could learn anything from him except that he liked making things.

The problem was the drying. Jar bottoms held water like a grudge, and Riley spent Friday hovering over it with a hair dryer borrowed from the front desk while his friend Maurice measured the display case with a tape measure and called out numbers. "Eleven inches of shelf," Maurice said. "Your jar's like nine. You're fine." The jar was earthenware; Riley knew that much from the bin's faded label, though he did not yet know why it would matter.

Chelsey arrived at four with a shoebox of porcelain cups, white as teeth, that she had thrown at the studio across town. Mr. Wiśniewski, the retired shop teacher who volunteered at the kiln two evenings a week, was supposed to load tonight's firing. Instead the front desk got a call, and a librarian came back to say he was in the hospital with his hip, nothing dramatic, but he would not be loading anything. "He left the key with instructions," she said, and held out an index card in his cramped handwriting, then drifted back toward the circulation desk.

The card gave temperatures. Riley read it twice, then dug the clay labels out of his backpack and laid them side by side on the worktable. His earthenware fired below about twelve hundred degrees Celsius. Chelsey's porcelain, according to the studio's stamp on the box flap, fired between twelve hundred and fourteen hundred. "They can't go in together," he said slowly, working it out aloud. "One load is one temperature. Mine can't take hers, and hers won't be done at mine." Chelsey leaned over the labels, chewing the end of her ponytail. "So we need two firings."

They did not have two firings. The kiln heated for hours and cooled for longer; if they loaded tonight, Saturday morning was the earliest the work came out, and even that was tight for the ten o'clock display. One load. That was the arithmetic, and Riley sat with it while the late sun came through the tall library windows and turned the whole room melancholic and gold, dust hanging in the light above the folding screen. He looked at his jar, then at Chelsey's cups, five of them, each one symmetrical in a way his coil-built jar would never be. She had been coming to the studio for two years. This was his first finished piece, and it happened to be a dead man's clay.

"Take yours," he said. Maurice looked up from the tape measure. "The jar's thick anyway, it might crack. Put the porcelain in." Chelsey said no, said he was being stupid, said they could flip a coin, and Riley said there was nothing to flip because she had actual skill and he had sentiment, and sentiment didn't need to be fired to be real. He said it fast, before it could get awkward, and started setting her cups on the kiln shelves with wadded newspaper under each foot. She stood beside him and handed him the next cup without another argument, which was its own kind of argument conceded.

They closed the kiln, turned the dial to the temperature on the studio's stamp, and Riley walked Chelsey and Maurice out through the lobby, past the front desk, past the display case already bearing a card that said STUDENT WORK with nothing in it yet. He came back for his backpack at closing and stood a minute in the darkened makerspace with his jar in his arms, still grey, still soft enough to mark with a thumbnail. It would sit in the case raw, beside the glossy cups, and he would let people think whatever they thought. He pressed the light switch with his elbow.

Saturday morning the librarian met him at the door, holding the phone away from her ear. "Good news, sort of," she said. "The show's been pushed to next Saturday. Budget thing, the case needs replacing." Riley stood there with the jar sweating against his chest, the whole careful sacrifice unspooling behind him, two loads suddenly possible, seven days of nothing but time. From the back room came the first tick of the cooling kiln, and Maurice, already there with the tape measure, called out, "Case is bigger, by the way."

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: Methane traps far more heat per molecule than carbon dioxide, but a methane molecule stays in the atmosphere for only about a decade on average, much less time than carbon dioxide.
story:
The kettle on her grandmother's stove had begun its low complaint before anyone spoke, and Isabelle spread the printouts across the kitchen table where the sunlight fell in a wide stripe. One page showed a graph, carbon dioxide measured decade by decade, the line climbing in small jagged steps like a staircase worn smooth at the edges. Neha leaned over it with her chin in her hand. Aditya sat across from them, arms folded, the way he sat when he intended to disagree before anyone had said anything.

"Mr. Rossi lent me this," Isabelle said. "From the college where he used to teach. He said the numbers themselves are simple, it's the picture that takes work." The paper had a laconic note in the corner, "Mauna Loa, in trust," which she'd had to look up; the measurements came from an observatory in Hawaii, and their provenance was longer than her whole life, longer than her grandmother's, air sampled month after month into a record nobody had planned to need this badly.

Neha traced the line upward with one finger, stopping at the last few years. "So this is the part we're living in. The top of the stairs." Her voice had a lightness that didn't quite hold, and Isabelle noticed how Neha kept her other hand in her lap, curled around her phone, off. Isabelle slid the plate of her grandmother's biscuits closer to her before saying anything, because Neha forgot to eat when she was nervous.

Aditya unfolded his arms long enough to pull the graph toward himself. "Fine, CO2 goes up. But my cousin works near the quarry, the gas plant past it, and he says half their maintenance is methane leaks, valves and flanges, and that if they just fixed those, that's the fastest fix there is. Methane's the real problem. Cut that first."

"That's not how it works," Isabelle said, more quickly than she meant to. "CO2 is the headline. The whole graph is CO2." She tapped the paper. Every news article she'd ever skimmed, every poster in the school hallway, had been carbon this and carbon that, and she had absorbed the hierarchy without ever checking it.

Neha looked up. "Actually wait. My physics teacher said something weird about methane in the spring. Something about it not lasting." She scrunched her face, reaching. "A methane molecule stays up there for about a decade on average. Ten years, and it's gone."

"Ten years," Aditya repeated, skeptical.

"Roughly a decade, she said. She wrote it on the board twice because she said people always forget it." Neha shrugged. "But she also said that per molecule, methane traps way more heat than CO2. Like, far more. That part I remember because it seemed backwards."

The kitchen went quiet except for the kettle's complaint rising toward a whistle. Isabelle turned the fact over the way her grandmother turned a stone in the garden, checking which side faced the sun. Methane was stronger but shorter-lived; carbon dioxide was weaker but, from the look of the graph, patient in a way that outlasted generations. She thought of her grandmother's jam shelf, the preserves that went fast because everyone loved them, and the honey that sat untouched for years and never spoiled. She almost said it aloud and decided the metaphor was too tidy.

"Okay," she said slowly. "So it's not which gas is the problem. It's which timescale you're asking about." She pulled a pencil from her bag and drew two quick lines on the back of the printout, one steep and short, one shallow and long. "If you cut methane leaks now, the molecules that are already up there clear out in about a decade, and the strong trapping stops soon after. That's the fast lever." She tapped the long line. "But CO2 keeps going. You'd have to cut it too, and keep it cut, or the staircase just keeps climbing."

Aditya was quiet for a moment, and she watched him change his mind, or at least loosen his grip on it. "So my cousin's not wrong," he said. "Fixing the leaks matters soon. Just not instead of."

"Not instead of," Neha agreed, and finally took a biscuit.

There was a knock at the door, and Mr. Rossi stood on the step in his cardigan, holding a small envelope of tomato seeds for the grandmother, an exchange they'd been conducting for years. He caught sight of the graph through the doorway and raised his eyebrows at Isabelle, a question rather than a lecture, which was why she'd asked him for the papers in the first place. He was the sort of teacher who stigmatized no question, not even the ones she felt foolish asking, like whether a gas could really be stronger and weaker at the same time.

"Did you settle it?" he asked.

"We settled that it doesn't settle," Isabelle said. "Methane for the next ten years. CO2 for everything after. And I can't tell from the graph which one deserves my worry first, so I'm going to worry about both."

Mr. Rossi smiled at the grandmother's herb pots on the sill as though they'd been consulted too. "That's a harder answer than most people want."

Her grandmother came through with the tea, set down four cups, and looked at the two lines Isabelle had drawn, steep and shallow, crossing near the top of the page like a signature. "Which one do I plant?" she asked, entirely seriously, and Isabelle picked up the pencil again.

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: In Agatha Christie's 1926 novel The Murder of Roger Ackroyd, the narrator, Dr Sheppard, turns out to be the murderer.
story:
Gabrielle had the novel in her lap on the school bus, thumb holding chapter one open, because Calum had ruined it for her and she was determined to catch him in the act of ruining it. He sat across the aisle with his feet on her backpack, which she allowed because he had lent her the book in the first place.

"You said you'd finished it," he said.

"I finished it at one in the morning. Now I'm going back to the beginning to find where he's lying."

"The whole point is you can't tell."

"Then I'll find where I can't tell. That's a place too."

Henri leaned over the seat in front of them, upside down basically, his tie hanging into Gabrielle's hair. He had read it two years ago at his cousin's house in Lyon and claimed to have guessed everything by page forty. Neither of them believed him, and this was a running argument with its own rituals.

"The narrator did it," Henri said. "Dr Sheppard. He's the murderer. I saw it coming."

"You saw nothing coming. You read the last chapter first, we all know."

"On my grandmother, I did not."

"Your grandmother," said Calum, "has a shelf of books with the endings already read. It's genetic."

Gabrielle ignored them, which took effort, and worked backward through the opening chapters. In chapter one Dr Sheppard sits at breakfast with his sister and then walks out to Ackroyd's house that evening, and she kept tripping over the sentence where he says something about the evening's work being done. It could mean the day's medical rounds. It could mean something worse. That was the trick, she decided: not lying, exactly. Choosing phrasings that were technically true and completely misleading. She read the line aloud to the others without telling them what she was doing, and both of them said "so?" at almost the same moment, which felt like proof.

"That's it," she said. "That's the mechanism. He never says he didn't do it. He says he couldn't have, in a tone that makes you believe him. The tone is doing the crime."

"You're describing every person I know," said Calum.

"I'm describing you specifically."

He pressed a hand to his chest, wounded, delighted. Somewhere behind them a freshman was trying to teach himself to whistle through his fingers and failing at volume, filling the bus with wet popping sounds, and the driver kept glancing in the mirror like a woman watching a science experiment she had not consented to.

The problem, and it bothered Gabrielle the way a pebble bothers a shoe, was that she had trusted the narrator completely, and she wanted to know whether that had been stupidity or design. If she reread the opening and found the hiding places, then Christie had played fair and Gabrielle had played lazy. If she found nothing, then the deck was stacked, and her trust had been manufactured without her consent. Those were two different books, really, and only one of them could she recommend to Ms. Lombardi, who ran the Thursday book club and had assigned her a presentation on point of view. Ms. Lombardi was famous for incisive questions, the kind that opened a discussion like a tin, and Gabrielle wanted at least one answer in her back pocket that wasn't a shrug.

"Here," she said suddenly, tapping a page. "Look at this. He narrates finding the body and he mentions everything except the one thing a murderer would need to hide, and he tells us what he was doing instead. But he never lets us check the time. The whole scene has no clock in it."

Calum took the book, read the paragraph, and gave it back with the expression of a man conceding a goal. "Fine. One hiding place. That doesn't mean the deck wasn't stacked."

"It means the deck was stacked in plain sight. Which is worse. Which is better. I haven't decided."

Henri said that in France this was called normal, and they explained to him, slowly, that this was why they kept him around, for statements like that, and he laughed his big laugh that turned three heads.

Gabrielle copied the page number into her notebook, then, after a pause, wrote a question beside it in small letters: does it matter that he told us, if we couldn't hear it? She underlined "hear" twice. Outside, the playing fields went by, then the car wash with the collapsing octopus on its roof, then the stop where the freshman got off, still whistling, quieter now but getting closer to something.

Calum nudged the book with his toe. "So what do you tell Lombardi on Thursday?"

"I tell her the reader and the narrator can both be telling the truth and the reader can still be wrong." She closed the notebook. "Then she'll ask me what responsibility the author had, and I'll say I'm still on the bus about that."

Henri frowned. "We get off in two stops."

"It's a metaphor, Henri."

"It's a bus," he said, and stood up anyway, holding out his hand for her bag.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Mise en place is a French cooking term meaning 'putting in place': measuring and preparing all the ingredients before starting to cook.
story:
Riley stood in the kitchen with his mother's notebook open to page sixty-three, where her handwriting turned small and certain: lemon cake, the one she made every August. He had decided at noon, without announcing it, that he would make it tonight while she was at her second shift, and that when she came home the house would smell the way it used to. He'd read the recipe twice. It seemed simple enough. Butter, sugar, flour, three eggs, lemon zest, milk. He set the oven to 350 and greased the pan the way she did, with a paper towel swiped around until the metal shone.

He creamed the butter and sugar until the mixture went pale and loose, scraped down the bowl, and felt something like competence settle over him. In the living room his father was on the phone with the bank again, his voice pitched low and careful, the way people speak when they are discussing solvency and do not want anyone else in the house to hear the word. Riley turned the radio up a notch to give him cover.

He sifted flour over the creamed butter. He grated the lemon against the window light, and the smell arrived so exactly that for a second he could see the montane trail above his uncle's village, the one they had hiked two summers ago, where wild thyme and citrus scrub grew out of the rock and the air tasted green. He stood there grating longer than the recipe required, just to keep the smell in the room.

Then he opened the refrigerator for the eggs and found the shelf holding only a jar of pickles, half an onion, and a folded paper bag of something that had once been greens. No eggs. Three eggs, the recipe said, and he read it again as if the number might revise itself out of pity. The batter sat behind him, flour half folded in, and the oven ticked upward toward temperature with the patience of something that had no opinion about him at all.

He texted Dave first, because Dave was two streets over. Dave replied with a photo of his own fridge, bare except for hot sauce, and the message "we are an eggless people." Then Riley stood at the counter wondering. Could he skip them? Could he use more milk? He had a vague sense that eggs did something, bound things, lifted things, but the vagueness itself was the problem. He didn't know what he didn't know, and the cake was already half-born.

He called Kassandra, who was the sort of person who read the whole manual before touching the machine. "You're stuck halfway through?" she said. "That's exactly why cooks do mise en place. It's French, it means putting in place, measuring and preparing everything before you start." She said her chef cousin drilled it into every new hire. "Nothing gets discovered at the worst moment, because there is no worst moment. Everything's already on the counter." Riley looked at his counter, where the flour bag leaned against the sugar canister like a friend who had arrived too late to help.

"I thought that was just for restaurants," he said. "Shows on TV, everything in little glass bowls."

"It's for anyone who doesn't want to be standing where you're standing right now," Kassandra said, and he could hear her smiling. "Go knock on a door. Somebody has eggs."

The door he knocked on, three houses down, belonged to Ms. Papadopoulos, who had watched him grow up from her porch and once excoriated the whole block, in a letter to the community newsletter, for letting the storm drains clog with leaves. She came to the door in a cardigan despite the heat. When he explained, holding the bowl of half-finished batter he had carried like an offering, she looked at it, then at him, and went inside without a word. She returned with four eggs in a blue bowl, not a carton, as if they were something to be lent gently.

"Bring the bowl back," she said. "And the cake. A slice. I knew your mother made that. You could smell it from here, some years." She paused at the threshold. "My mother never wrote anything down. Everything in her hands and her head, all at once. When she died, all of it went with her." She said it without sorrow, more like a fact about the weather, and closed the door.

Back in his kitchen, Riley cracked the three eggs into the batter and watched them disappear into the flour as he folded, and the cake went into the oven on time after all. While it baked he sat at the table with his mother's notebook and thought about the two ways of doing things. Kassandra's way, everything measured and certain before you begin, seemed safe and also a little cold, like a recipe that could never surprise you. His mother's way, the way he had charged in tonight, had given him the lemon smell and the memory of the trail, and also twenty minutes of genuine fear. Maybe, he thought, the point wasn't choosing one. Maybe you set out what you can, and accept that some things you only discover standing in front of an empty shelf, and that the discovering is not the disaster, it's just the part the recipe doesn't mention. He wasn't sure. He wrote "eggs" at the bottom of page sixty-three in his own handwriting, next to hers, so the notebook now held both of them.

When his mother came in at nine, tired and still wearing her name tag, she stopped in the doorway and breathed in. Riley slid the last slice onto the blue bowl's saucer, which he had washed and dried, and held it out to her. "One's for Ms. Papadopoulos," he said. "That's hers to return."

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: When muscle cells run low on oxygen, they convert pyruvate into lactate, which regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can continue making 2 ATP per glucose.
story:
The trail behind the school cut through a strip of birch and then opened onto the Hutchins farm, where the grass grew long and the path dissolved into a suggestion of a path. Clara had chosen it because the library made her feel watched and her bedroom made her feel asleep. She walked with the textbook wedged open against her forearm, index cards fanned in her other hand, reading aloud in a low mutter the way other people prayed.

Benoit caught up to her at the second fence post, breathing hard from the hill. "You're studying outside now. That's a new level of desperation."

"I'm studying in a location with oxygen," Clara said. "Unlike my cells, apparently." She held up a card. Pyruvate, lactate, NAD+. The terms had been circling each other all week without mating.

Luciano arrived at a jog, coat unzipped, carrying nothing, which was how Luciano carried everything. "Ms. Oyelaran says the test is fair," he said. "Which means it's not fair, it's just honest about being unfair."

"There's a difference?" Benoit asked.

"There's a difference," Luciano said, and left it there, the way he did with things he wanted them to chew on.

They came out of the trees into the field, and Benoit, who could not be near an open space without racing across it, pointed at the far gate. "First one there." He was gone before Clara agreed to anything, and Luciano laughed and followed, and Clara, annoyed at being left, stuffed the cards in her pocket and ran.

The grass was recalcitrant, catching at her ankles, and halfway across the field her thighs began to burn, that deep sour heat she knew from track but had never thought about, really thought about. She kept going. At the gate she arrived last, bent over, hands on her knees, and while Benoit whooped and Luciano leaned against the post pretending he hadn't tried, Clara stared at the ground and felt her legs throbbing and heard herself say, "That's lactate."

"What?" Benoit said.

"My legs. The burning." She straightened up, still gulping air. "When the muscle cells run low on oxygen, they convert pyruvate into lactate."

Luciano pushed off the post. "Why would they do that to you?"

"It's not to me." She pulled the cards out of her pocket, found the one she wanted, the creased one she'd rewritten three times. "It regenerates NAD+. So glycolysis can keep going. Two ATP per glucose." She said it slowly, testing it against her own aching legs. "It's not a punishment. It's a rescue that hurts."

"Everything you say sounds like a riddle," Benoit said, but he was rubbing his own quadriceps now, frowning at them as if they'd been keeping secrets.

They walked back along the fence line, and Clara found that the walking helped, that the field was teaching her something the library never had. The ache was data. She had read the lactate fact forty times and forgotten it forty times because it sat inert on the card, but here it lived in her body, in the specific heat still fading from her calves, and she understood that she had been trying to memorize the cell instead of imagining it. She tried to hold both ways at once: the diagram, clean and numbered, and this field, muddy and personal. The diagram gave her the sequence. The field gave her the reason to care. Neither was enough alone, and she could not yet say how they fit together, only that she wanted to hold them together, even sloppily, even if the exam rewarded only one.

"You look like you're either enlightened or nauseous," Luciano said.

"Both. Possibly." She dealt the cards to them like a dealer at a corrupt casino: pyruvate to Benoit, NAD+ to Luciano, kept glucose for herself. "Race back. Whoever gets to the birches first explains their card. Out loud. In a sentence."

"That's the worst game I've ever heard," Benoit said, and lined up at the fence anyway.

Ms. Oyelaran was coming down the trail from the other direction with her dog, and she watched them crouch at the line and raised an eyebrow at Clara. "Studying, or tormenting?"

"Same thing today," Clara said.

"I'll offer amnesty to whoever loses," Ms. Oyelaran said, and the dog, indifferent to biochemistry, lunged at a stick.

They ran. Clara's legs objected immediately, the lactate still there, or the memory of it, and she let the burn become information instead of misery, one foot and then the other, glucose splitting somewhere inside her, the little Two ATP per glucose, she thought, the small steady ration that keeps everything going. Luciano reached the birches first by half a stride, and he turned around, breathless, holding up the card.

"NAD plus," he said. "It comes back. That's all I've got."

"That's most of it," Clara said, and she could hear how much she meant it. Benoit was still twenty feet out, waving the pyruvate card over his head like a surrender.

"Read it to me when I get there," he called. "Slowly. Twice."

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: Without its natural greenhouse effect, Earth's average surface temperature would be about minus 18 degrees Celsius instead of roughly 14 degrees Celsius.
story:
Grandfather's house smelled of cedar and burnt coffee, and Jordan had claimed the kitchen table by nine, which he would later describe to Hailee as a heroic act of discipline, though the truth was that his bedroom had no air conditioning and the table was under a ceiling fan. He spread out the graph Mr. Pelletier had handed back to him, the one with the red ink circling the caption "explain in your own words," and he set his phone against the sugar bowl with Hailee's face already waiting on the screen.

"You failed a graph," Hailee said, delighted. "How do you fail a graph. It's a line."

"I didn't fail it. I under-explained it." Jordan smoothed the page where the fan's breeze made it undulate like something alive. "Mr. Pelletier says I described it instead of explaining it. He says describing is what you do when you don't understand, and explaining is what you do when you do."

"That's the most French-teacher thing a science teacher has ever said."

From the doorway, Grandfather, who claimed to be hard of hearing only when it suited him, said, "When I was seventeen I had to memorize the kings of England. At least your line goes somewhere." He put down a plate of peaches and retreated to his recliner, where he pretended to read and actually eavesdropped, a fact Jordan knew perfectly well and pretended not to.

Here is what Jordan had written, and what he now believed, with total confidence, to be true: greenhouse gases were the villains, the line on the graph was the evidence, and anyone who said otherwise was running chicanery for the oil companies. He said all of this to Hailee in a single breath, tapping the page so hard the phone wobbled.

Hailee, to her credit, only looked at him for a moment. Then she called Melanie in, three faces stacked on the screen like a committee, and Melanie said, "Okay, but we watched that planetarium thing in eighth grade. The Moon part."

"What Moon part."

"The part where the Moon swings between boiling and freezing because it has no atmosphere, and Earth has one, and the guy said without its natural greenhouse effect Earth's average surface temperature would be about minus 18 degrees Celsius instead of roughly 14." She said it flatly, like reciting a locker combination. "So greenhouse gases are also the reason we're not a snowball. That's the whole trick of the assignment. Both things are true."

Jordan opened his mouth to say that was wrong, then closed it, because it wasn't wrong, and he could feel that it wasn't wrong, the way you feel a stair that isn't there. He looked at the graph again. The line climbed in its patient sawtooth way, decade over decade, and he had been so busy hating it that he had never once asked what the flat parts would have meant, or what the world would have been before the climbing started. Fourteen degrees was not a default. Fourteen degrees was a gift with a clause in it.

"So it's not that greenhouse gases are bad," he said slowly, testing each word like a plank over a creek. "It's that they're necessary and we've been adding more, and the graph is the receipt for the adding. I got the receipt and thought it was the crime."

"That's very poetic," Hailee said. "Put it in the retake and Mr. Pelletier will weep."

"He might weep anyway." Jordan pulled the peaches closer and ate one, dripping, thinking that the hard part was not the science. The hard part was holding two ideas without dropping either: that the atmosphere was the reason anything lived, and that the same atmosphere was changing in a way the graph measured. He would say that part out loud tomorrow, uncertain bits included, because pretending certainty had been the actual failure all along. He was aware that this sounded noble, and that an hour ago he had been certain of the opposite thing with exactly the same confidence, so his confidence was clearly not to be trusted, and he said so.

"That's growth," Melanie said, "or fatigue."

"Both," said Grandfather from the recliner, not looking up from his book.

Jordan laughed, wiped peach juice on his sleeve, and wrote across the top of the graph, in handwriting that would have horrified Mr. Pelletier: minus 18 versus 14, then underneath it, why the difference matters twice. He held the page up to the phone so both girls could see, and Hailee said, "Still just a line, buddy," and he turned off the fan to keep it still.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: The Chicago Manual of Style, whose notes-and-bibliography system uses footnotes, was first published by the University of Chicago Press in 1906.
story:
Elizabeth had claimed the corner table by the microfilm cabinet because its outlet worked and nobody else wanted it, which was the only kind of inheritance she had ever received. Spread before her were four books on the Homestead Strike, a stack of index cards, and a photocopied page titled "Notes and Bibliography: The Chicago Style," which Ms. Byrne had handed her at the reference desk three days earlier with the words, "Start here. You can fight with it later." She was fighting with it now.

The problem was not the argument. She had one, more or less: the standard textbook version of the strike gave Carnegie and Frick the last word, and the popular newspapers of 1892 had done the same, and she suspected the paper could show how. The problem was that every time she made a claim, the style sheet demanded she stop, raise a little number, and prove where the claim had come from. It felt like being interrupted by herself.

Grady dropped into the chair across from her with a granola bar and his own stack of sources. "Tell me again why I can't just put the web address at the end."

"Because you're making an argument," Elizabeth said. "Not a collage."

"That's not an answer." He peeled the wrapper down and pointed at her page of typed note cards. "Look at this. Number four, number five, number six. Half my essay is going to be numbers."

She turned the style sheet around so he could read the top line. "The Chicago Manual of Style," she said. "That's what this is. The notes-and-bibliography system, footnotes at the bottom of the page. It's from the University of Chicago Press."

"So it's a book of rules."

"It was first published in 1906," she said. "It's older than your great-grandparents."

Grady sat back. He did the arithmetic visibly, the way some people do, lips moving. "My great-grandmother Rose is ninety-two. So her parents." He looked at the sheet again with something that was not quite respect. "A hundred and some years of people arguing about where the comma goes."

That evening, and on the two evenings after, Elizabeth discovered that the comma had its own syntax, a small grammar of author, title, city, publisher, year, and that she could not break it without the entry collapsing into noise. She also discovered that footnotes did something the bibliography alone could not do. A footnote could whisper. It could say, in small type at the bottom of page three, "See also the account in the Pittsburgh Dispatch, which disagrees," and go on letting the sentence above it stand. She began to understand that there were two kinds of people in the world, which was a lie she told herself anyway: people who thought evidence shut the door, and people who thought it opened one more.

Eden had been in the second group once, or seemed to have been, back when the two of them ran the debate club together and disagreed for sport. That had ended in the spring, over a question of who got to go to regionals, and Elizabeth had chosen the team list without asking her, and Eden had chosen not to speak to her for a month. Elizabeth still could not decide, on the walk to the library on Thursday, whether deciding alone had been efficiency or cowardice. She put the question away the way she now put caveats in footnotes: noted, deferred, unresolved.

Eden was there when she arrived, at the other end of the long table, headphones on, a laptop open to what was unmistakably the same assignment. Elizabeth almost kept walking. Instead she set her bag down at the corner and said, "I found out the manual's older than our great-grandparents. I'm thinking of proselytizing."

Eden pulled out one earbud. "Proselytizing what?"

"Footnotes. Chicago style. There's a whole system where you raise a number and the number tells the truth for you."

"I'm using MLA," Eden said. "In-text, parenthetical, done."

"That's not the same. Yours shouts in the middle of the sentence. Mine waits at the bottom of the page like a civilized person."

Eden looked at her for a moment, and something in the look was regionalals, or the strike, or the whole spring. "You realize you're describing yourself," she said. "The person who waits at the bottom of the page. Or the person who doesn't."

Elizabeth laughed before she could decide whether it was funny. "Ms. Byrne would say the manual doesn't care about our character. It just wants the commas in the right place."

Ms. Byrne, arriving to reshelve a cart of returns, paused at the end of the table. "It cares a little," she said. She straightened the stack of Elizabeth's books, spines out, unasked. "The whole point of a citation is that a hostile reader can follow you. Even a sectarian one, convinced you're wrong about everything. You lay the trail so they can check." She pushed the cart on toward American history.

Elizabeth sat back down. She opened her draft to page two, where her best sentence stood, the one about Carnegie getting the last word, and beneath it she raised a small four and began, in the proper syntax, to lay her trail: author, comma, title, comma, the rest. Then she flipped to the bibliography and found that entry number four there had no publisher listed, and, under it, that she had cited the same book twice under two different spellings of the author's name, and, further down, in the entry she had been proudest of, that the date read 1982 for a newspaper that had folded in 1938.

She raised her hand halfway, the old reflex from class, before remembering where she was, and Eden, without looking up, slid her own MLA handbook down the table to her.

activity: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
knowledge_domain: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
fact: A lawyer who types faster than her assistant still gains by hiring him to type, because every hour she spends typing is an hour of better-paid legal work given up.
story:
The lemonade stand sat at the end of Mr. Kerr's driveway because his corner got the traffic from the pool, and because Mr. Kerr had agreed to lend a folding table in exchange for one free cup, an arrangement Brooklyn had negotiated herself and now regretted, since he came back for refills.

She was there because she was failing economics, and because her mother had said that if Brooklyn wanted the sixty dollars for the study group's review book, she could raise some of it herself. Ruth was there because Ruth liked sitting outside and considered the stand a social event that occasionally produced money. Felicity was there because Felicity had already read the chapter twice and could not understand why the others hadn't.

"Comparative advantage," Felicity said, fanning herself with the textbook. "It's on the exam Thursday."

"That's not an explanation," Brooklyn said. "That's a label with an attitude."

Felicity turned the pitcher so the ice caught the light, which did not presage anything good. "Okay. Say there's a lawyer. She types faster than her assistant. Faster. Better at typing than the guy she pays to type."

"Then she's an idiot for paying him," Ruth said. A man in a pool shirt bought two cups and waited, interested, while Felicity counted his change.

"That's what I said," Brooklyn said. "That's exactly what I said to Mr. Kerr, and he gave me that look he gives when you've done the reading but not the thinking."

Felicity closed the book on her thumb. "It's not about typing. Every hour the lawyer spends typing is an hour of legal work she's not doing. Better-paid legal work. So she gives up more when she types than he does. She's better at both things, and she still gains by hiring him."

Ruth frowned into her cup. "So the assistant isn't better at anything."

"He's better at being cheap to use," Felicity said. "His typing costs less, because he isn't giving up a lawyer's wages to do it."

Brooklyn kept making change for a woman with a stroller while this worked through her. It reminded her of something, and it took her most of the afternoon to decide what: her tutoring business. She tutored middle schoolers in math at twenty dollars an hour, and she did her own scheduling, emailing parents and shuffling time slots, which she was genuinely fast at. She was faster than her little brother, who had offered to do it for three dollars an hour and whom she had turned down, telling him that if you wanted something done right, you did it yourself. It had sounded like wisdom at the time. Now it sat in her stomach like a wrong answer she had written in pen.

"Say I spend two hours a week on scheduling," she said, wiping down the table. "Two hours I'm not tutoring. My brother would take four hours, and he'd do it worse, and he'd still be cheaper, because his four hours aren't worth anything else to anybody."

"That's the whole thing," Felicity said. "Two people trade and both get richer, even if one of them is better at everything. It's why countries do it."

"Then why does it feel like cheating the little brother?"

"Because you're confusing kindness with arithmetic," Ruth said, which was more discernment than Ruth usually offered before five o'clock.

Brooklyn wasn't sure it was that simple. There was something in the argument that felt specious, some slick move from money to wellbeing, and she couldn't put her finger on where the slide happened. Her brother's four hours weren't worth nothing to him; they were worth bike rides and boredom and whatever else a twelve-year-old's afternoon held. But then, she thought, the parents would pay her either way, and the middle schoolers would get their hours either way, and she would get two hours back to earn forty dollars and pay him twelve and keep twenty-eight. It still felt like the numbers were leaving something out, and she was honest enough with herself to admit she didn't know what, or whether it was anything more than the vague suspicion that anything explained this cleanly deserved suspicion.

Mr. Kerr came back with his cup, his third, and stood there in the late sun with his toes in flip-flops. "Learn anything today?"

"I learned that I should have charged you per refill," Brooklyn said. "You had an absolute advantage at taking free lemonade the whole time."

He laughed, and she poured him half a cup anyway, and she took out her phone and started typing a message to her brother, deleted it, and typed a better one.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: US food safety guidance says perishable food should not sit between 40 and 140 degrees Fahrenheit for more than two hours, or one hour when it is above 90 degrees.
story:
The farmers' market had already begun to sweat by nine, the tents gone soft overhead and the asphalt throwing heat back at Sophia's shins. She carried a canvas bag with a whole chicken wrapped in butcher paper, a jar of cream, and a bundle of basil, and she had until six to turn it into dinner, because her mother had taken the late shift and had said, with the particular confidence of someone leaving the house, "You'll handle it, you're better at this than I am anyway." Reece had agreed to come along for the tomatoes, which he claimed he could taste the difference in, though he spent most of the first hour sitting on a curb eating a pastry.

They drifted past Ms. Tang's stall, where the tomatoes were stacked in flat crates like something being guarded. Sophia had bought from her for two summers, and Ms. Tang always weighed quickly and never made small talk until the very end, when she would say something that stayed with Sophia for the rest of the day. Today it was, "You have a chicken in that bag." Sophia said yes, dinner for the family. Ms. Tang put the tomatoes in a paper sack and said, "It's ninety-four already," and turned to her next customer, and Sophia stood there for a second feeling the sentence settle somewhere uncomfortable.

Reece was nonchalant about it when she mentioned it. "People buy chicken at markets all the time," he said, gesture taking in the whole crowded lane, the heat-drunk families, the man selling honey with his shirt stuck to his back. "If it were a real problem there'd be signs or something." Sophia wanted to believe him, partly because the chicken had cost eleven dollars and partly because Reece's certainty was easier to borrow than her own. They walked the length of the market twice more, stopping for lemonade, listening to a fiddler, and by the time they reached the shade of the oak at the far end, a general malaise had spread through her, the kind that comes from standing in heat with a task waiting at home.

She took out her phone and searched for how long raw chicken could sit out in the heat. The answer came up immediately and was plainer than she expected: perishable food should not sit between 40 and 140 degrees Fahrenheit for more than two hours, or more than one hour when the temperature is above 90. She read it twice, then looked at the weather app, which said 96, and then at her own bag, sitting on the grass in the sun, and did the arithmetic she had been avoiding. She'd bought the chicken at the second stall of the day, right at the start. It had been in that bag, in this heat, for over an hour already, and home was a twenty-minute drive with no air conditioning in her mother's old car.

"That's not nothing," she said, and handed him the phone.

Reece read it and tried to contextualize it the way he contextualized everything, folding it into a bigger picture until it looked smaller. "Okay, but the paper's thick, and it's not like it was on the dashboard." He looked at the number again, though, 40 to 140, one hour above 90, and she watched something move behind his face. "You've still got like ten minutes of margin," he said, but he said it slower, and then he said, "If it's even accurate." A beat. "It's from a government food safety page, Reece. It's not a blog." He handed the phone back and, after a moment, said, "Yeah. Don't cook it."

Driving home, Sophia kept the chicken on the floor of the passenger side with the windows down, which felt absurd, like closing a gate after the horse, and she understood even as she did it that she was performing diligence for an audience of one. In the kitchen she laid out what she actually had: Ms. Tang's tomatoes, some of them split and ugly and smelling like summer itself, a bag of dried pasta, garlic, the cream, which had stayed sealed and had been in the shade the whole time, a wedge of parmesan, and half a loaf of bread going stale. She put the chicken in the trash, pressing it down under the coffee grounds, and stood at the counter with her hands flat on the tile.

The problem, as she saw it, was that Reece's way of thinking and hers weren't really opposites. His instinct was that risk was everywhere and mostly survivable; hers was that risk could be known and therefore managed. But the page on her phone hadn't told her the chicken was spoiled, only that it had entered the territory where spoilish risk was real and unmeasurable from a kitchen, and that was the part neither of them could argue their way around. She didn't know. She would never know. What she knew was the boundary, and the boundary had been crossed before she'd even thought to look for it.

She cut the tomatoes into wedges, salted them hard, and let them drain while the water heated, then mashed them roughly with garlic and torn basil and a slow pour of cream, tasting until the sauce stopped tasting like a fallback and started tasting like a decision. She toasted the stale bread with olive oil and salt for crumbs. The pasta came together fast, faster than the roast chicken would have, and by the time her mother's headlights swept the kitchen wall, there were four plates on the table because Reece had texted that he was coming by to see whether she'd actually thrown it out.

"I threw it out," she said at the door, and he held up a bag of the market's peaches, which had also spent an hour in his backpack in the sun, and they both looked at the bag for a long moment. "An hour exactly," he said. "Maybe fifty-five minutes." They carried the peaches inside, cold water running over them in the sink, and behind them her mother was already lifting a fork from the pot, saying, "You made this?" and Sophia said, "Sit down, it's still hot," and turned off the tap.

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: The SIFT method from educator Mike Caulfield stands for Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, and Trace claims to their original context.
story:
The video arrived during third period, passed from phone to phone under desks like contraband. It showed a crowd of students outside a school, some of them shoving a banner into a trash can while someone off camera laughed, and the caption beneath it said it had happened at Hendricks High that morning. Mia watched it twice, felt her stomach tighten with something that was almost pleasure, this close to outrage, and sent it to her group chat before the bell had even finished ringing.

By lunch, half the sophomore class had seen it. Will was pacing beside the vending machines, saying we should do something, and Cedric was already typing a post with words like disgusting and unforgivable. "Everyone's sharing it," he said, not looking up. "If we don't say anything, we're basically fine with it." Mia nodded along, though she had already begun, in the back of her mind, to rewrite the morning. In her memory she had hesitated before sending. In her memory she had almost texted her cousin at Hendricks first.

The doubt arrived quietly, the way a sullen weather front settles over a field without asking permission. She was standing in the library during study hall, pretending to work on her history outline, when she noticed that the crowd in the video was wearing shorts. It was November. She pulled the video back up and looked again: bare legs, short sleeves, a green tree in full leaf behind the fence. Nobody in the frame was cold.

She glanced at the study carrel next to hers, where a printed handout sat abandoned, something Mr. Farah-Ali had left beside the printer weeks ago and never collected. At the bottom of the page, under a heading she hadn't read before, four steps were laid out in plain type. Cedric leaned over her shoulder, having followed her in. "What's that?" he asked. "SIFT," she said, reading the word off the page. Then, half to herself, she read the rest: "Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, Trace claims to their original context."

Stop was the hardest part. She wanted, more than she could admit, for the video to be exactly what the caption said, because she had already invested her whole afternoon in being angry about it. But she screenshotted a frame and dropped it into a reverse image search, her fingers slower now, deliberate, as though the library had grown quieter around her. The results loaded. The same image, and then the same image again, on a page dated two summers ago, from a town three states away, attached to a story about a prank week that had ended without any banners being harmed at all. The video wasn't lying, exactly. It had simply been picked up and moved, like a word transliterated from one alphabet to another, its shape intact and its meaning gone.

"Delete your post," she said to Cedric, and he looked at her with the flat expression of someone who has typed a paragraph in public and does not want to take it back. "It's fake," she said. "Not fake. Old and from somewhere else. I searched it." He argued for a while, the way people argue when the argument has already collapsed: everyone else is sharing it, someone would have caught it if it were wrong, you can't even tell with these things. Will just stood by the window with his arms crossed, watching them both, saying nothing, which Mia understood was its own kind of answer.

She wrote a correction and then sat with it, cursor blinking, because a correction felt like a confession. She had been part of it. Her share had been one click in a chain, and the chain had gone out from her phone into a hundred others, and complicity, she understood now, did not require intent, only speed. She posted it anyway, with the screenshot of the two dates side by side, and watched the little notifications begin.

What she could not figure out, walking out past the vending machines toward the buses, was the account that had first posted it, the one with no picture and a handle made of consonants, which had known exactly what November anger would do with a summer video. She stopped at the corner and looked the account up one more time. The page was gone, or had never been there, and the wind was pushing a paper cup along the curb in front of her when Cedric caught up and said, "So what do we do the next time one shows up?"

activity: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
knowledge_domain: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
fact: In her 1997 essay on leverage points, Donella Meadows argued that adjusting numbers like taxes or subsidies rarely changes a system much, while changing its goals or underlying paradigm changes the most.
story:
The seminar room smelled like wet rain jackets and instant coffee, and Jeremy had spent his bus ride memorizing a number: eight dollars. That was the fee he wanted the city to charge for parking downtown, up from five, and he had eleven sources to prove it would work. He spread them across the table like a hand of cards.

Mr. Okonkwo had set the question two weeks ago: should the city raise the downtown parking fee to cut traffic and fund the bus system? Jeremy had drawn the yes side, and Braydon had drawn the no side, which was convenient, because Braydon argued the way he played defense in hockey, all shoulders and no plan. Gurleen had drawn the wild card role, questioner, which meant she could attack either of them and, by tradition, would attack both.

Braydon went first and spent four minutes on small businesses. Five dollars was already a tax on shops, he said, and eight would be a guillotine. He had a graph with arrows on it. Then it was Jeremy's turn, and he laid out the numbers: revenue projections, traffic counts from three cities, a table where he had tried to parametrize the whole problem, fee on one axis, ridership on the other, as if the downtown were an equation he could solve by choosing the right coefficient.

Gurleen's hand went up before he finished his second slide.

"What if you set it at ten?" she said. "Or twelve? If eight is good, more is better, right? Or does the system break somewhere?"

"Twelve would be politically impossible," Jeremy said.

"So the number isn't really the lever. Politics is."

He said something about elasticity and moved on, but the sentence stuck to him like a burr. During the break he stood by the window, where the rain had turned the parking lot into an archipelago of gray puddles and parked cars, each one paying five dollars a day to be there.

Mr. Okonkwo drifted past carrying a stack of photocopies, and Jeremy noticed one had a title in big letters across the top: leverage points. Below it, a name, Donella Meadows, and a date, 1997. When Mr. Okonkwo set the stack down to answer someone's question about citations, Jeremy slid the top copy off and read it while pretending to check his phone.

The essay said something that rearranged the furniture in his head. Meadows argued that adjusting numbers like taxes or subsidies rarely changes a system much. Changing a system's goals changed it more. Changing its underlying paradigm, the deep story everyone silently agreed to, changed it the most. Jeremy read the paragraph twice, then looked out at the lot again. The city council was spending its evenings arguing five dollars versus eight, and according to this essay, that was the weakest kind of change there was. The whole debate was a fight over the dial on a machine whose purpose nobody was questioning. The paradigm under the parking lot was that a person in a car is the default citizen of downtown, and every fee, every subsidy, every number existed to serve that story.

He went back to the table with his notes but didn't open them.

When the seminar resumed, Braydon was ready for him, armed with a counter-projection showing that at eight dollars, drivers would park in the residential streets for free and walk, shifting the problem rather than shrinking it. Under the old plan, this would have launched Jeremy into a rebuttal about boundary pricing. Instead he heard himself say, "You're right, probably."

Braydon blinked. "I am?"

"At eight, or five, or twelve. We could argue the number all afternoon and it wouldn't matter much." He tapped the photocopy. "There's this essay. 1997, Donella Meadows. She called the deep ones leverage points. Her point was that tweaking numbers, taxes, subsidies, rarely changes a system much, but changing its goals or its paradigm changes the most. So the fee debate is the weakest thing we could be fighting about."

"So what do we do," Braydon said, "abolish parking?"

"I don't know," Jeremy said, and was surprised by how much he liked saying it. "Maybe the goal isn't cheaper parking or pricier parking. Maybe the goal is that a kid with a bus pass counts the same as a guy in a truck. If the city actually believed that, the fee would set itself. But I can't tell you what number comes out, because I don't know yet, and I'm not sure anyone does."

Gurleen wrote something in her notebook and didn't attack him, which from her was a standing ovation.

Mr. Okonkwo collected the photocopies at the end of class, counting them, and paused at Jeremy with the stack hugged to his chest. He didn't say anything about the one that had migrated across the room. He only asked, "Same side next time, or do you want to argue against yourself?"

"I want the questioner seat," Jeremy said.

Outside, the rain had thinned to a diaphanous mist over the parking lot, and Jeremy stood under the awning watching a woman feed five dollars into a meter, quarters at a time, patient as a ritual. He took out his phone and opened the city council's website, found the agenda for Tuesday's meeting, and started typing a request to speak.

"Are you actually going?" Gurleen said, appearing beside him with her hood up.

"Three minutes at the microphone," Jeremy said. "I figure I'll spend one of them on the fee, and two on the machine."

He hit submit, and the confirmation page loaded slowly, like even the system was thinking it over.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: A 1950 study by Leon Festinger, Stanley Schachter and Kurt Back in student housing found that people living closer together, or near shared stairways, were more likely to become friends.
story:
The last box went into the trunk at six in the morning, and Morgan sat in the back seat with her backpack between her knees while her mother checked the mirrors twice, then a third time, as though the car had grown heavier overnight. Fourteen hours to Weldon, Ohio. The seats were already stiff from the drive's first hour, and Morgan had the psych textbook she'd borrowed from Ms. Kang open on her lap, not to read so much as to hold.

She had taken it out of Ms. Kang's classroom bookshelf on the last day of school, and Ms. Kang had said, keep it, I have two copies, which was a lie Morgan recognized and accepted, the way you accept a gift someone insists is not a gift. The bookmark was a receipt from the diner where Gillian had worked Saturdays.

"You're going to read the whole way?" her mother asked.

"I'm going to look at it the whole way."

The night before, Gillian had come over with a plastic bag of parting things: a half bottle of nail polish, a photograph from freshman year, a mix CD that nothing in the new house would play. "Promise you'll come back for spring break," Gillian had said. "Not, like, we'll see. An actual promise." Gillian wanted the promise more than she wanted to admit, Morgan could tell, because she kept folding the top of the bag over and over while she asked. Morgan had said, "I promise," and meant it, and also knew that promises like that were the kind people made to underwrite a distance they hadn't crossed yet. Gillian had hugged her hard enough to hurt, and Maximus, who had driven her over, sat in the idling car outside with the hazards on and never got out, which was its own kind of goodbye, a deliberate one.

Now, somewhere past the state line, Morgan turned to the chapter she'd flagged with the receipt. She had read it once already, at the kitchen table at midnight while her mother taped boxes. A 1950 study by Leon Festinger, Stanley Schachter and Kurt Back, done in student housing, had found that people living closer together, or near shared stairways, were more likely to become friends. She read it again anyway, slowly, the way you reread a text message before you decide what to answer.

"Listen to this," she said. "A 1950 study. Leon Festinger, Stanley Schachter, Kurt Back. In student housing. People living closer together, or near shared stairways, were more likely to become friends."

"What's that mean?"

"It means it's not about who people are. It's about where they are. My whole friendship with Gillian started because her locker was next to mine." She paused. "And Maximus lived two houses down. And Ms. Kang's classroom was the one by the stairs."

Her mother was quiet for a mile. "So you're saying friendship is just geography."

"I'm saying it's not only character. Or effort. It might be stairs." Morgan closed the book partway and looked out the window at a water tower with a faded mascot painted on it. There was something in the finding that should have been comforting, she thought, if you were moving to a new town, that friends could be a function of proximity, that all she had to do was be near people. But there was something in it that was also a small act of theft. It took the story she and Gillian told about themselves, the one about choosing each other, and made it look like an accident of lockers. She turned the receipt over in her fingers. She could hold both ideas, she decided, the way you hold a book open to two pages at once, and she did not have to resolve which one was true. Maybe the choosing mattered and the stairs mattered. Maybe you chose harder once the stairs had done their part.

Gillian's spring break promise sat in her mind next to the study, and the two did not argue with each other exactly, but they leaned. If friendship needed closeness, a promise across four hundred miles was working against the grain of the whole finding. If friendship was choice, the promise was everything.

"Can I see the map?" Morgan asked. Her mother passed her phone back over the seat. Morgan found Weldon and zoomed in until the streets resolved into names, and she located the high school, then the street they would live on, then, two blocks over, a library with a set of broad front steps where, presumably, people came and went. She set a pin on it.

"That where you'll be going?" her mother asked.

"That's where the stairs are," Morgan said, and turned the textbook to the blank inside cover, and began writing a note to leave for the next person who took it from a shelf.

"Dear whoever," she wrote, and then stopped, and chewed the pen, and looked out the window at the water tower shrinking behind them.

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: Most of Emily Brontë's Wuthering Heights, published in 1847, is told by the housekeeper Nelly Dean to the visitor Lockwood, so events reach readers through two narrators with their own biases.
story:
The essay was due on Friday, and Colton had written nothing but his name. He sat in the back row of Ms. Pierre's classroom with Wuthering Heights open to the wrong page, listening to Khloe argue with the boy across the aisle about whether Heathcliff deserved sympathy. Khloe said obviously not, he hung a dog. The other boy said that was Nelly's version of events, and Colton felt something shift, small and inchoate, at the back of his thinking.

"Wait," he said, and both of them turned, because he rarely spoke in this class. "Who actually tells us Heathcliff hung the dog?"

Khloe frowned at him. "The book."

"But who." He flipped to the front, then further, hunting through the pages he had highlighted in a kind of mechanical panic two nights ago. "Lockwood writes it down, right?
