He's the visitor, he's the one keeping the diary. But he's not the one who saw it. He's getting all of it secondhand from the housekeeper."

"Nelly Dean," the other boy said. "Most of the book is her talking to him."

"Then everything we know comes through both of them." Colton heard his own voice speed up. "First she decides what happened, then he decides what to write down of what she said. Two sets of hands on every fact."

Ms. Pierre, who had been watering the fern by the window as though the conversation had nothing to do with her, set down the can. "Keep going, Colton."

He didn't want to keep going. He had spent the whole first week of the unit skimming, and now he was embarrassed by how late this was arriving. But he remembered a Tuesday in September when he'd told his father that a kid on his soccer team had quit out of laziness, and his father had later heard from the coach that the kid was working nights to help his family, and Colton had never corrected the story with anyone except Khloe. He had just let the lazy version stand, because it was simpler and because he had wanted to be angry instead of uncertain.

He said none of that. He said, "Nelly doesn't like Heathcliff. She says it, more than once. She thinks he's cruel and greedy and she wants the Earnshaws to come out ahead. So when she tells Lockwood what he did, how much of the shape of it is her?"

"Whether her dislike colours the whole story," Khloe said slowly, "that's the question."

"And Lockwood barely pushes back. He just writes it down like she's a window instead of a person." Colton looked at the highlighted pages, the yellow streaks he'd laid down without asking who was talking. "I believed all of it. I read it like it was just true."

The class was quiet in the way it got when someone had said something that reorganized the room. Ms. Pierre asked whether the same suspicion should apply to any narrator, and Anya said probably yes, and then a boy near the window said that if you couldn't trust anyone you couldn't trust anything, which started a small argument about whether doubting every source meant abrogating your responsibility to have any beliefs at all. Colton listened without joining in. He had a notebook open now, and he was writing questions instead of answers. Which events did Nelly witness directly? Which did she only hear about? Where did she have something to lose?

At lunch he sat with Khloe in the stairwell by the gym, the book between them, and they went through the early chapters chapter by chapter. Nelly was there for almost everything, Khloe pointed out; she was in the kitchen and the doorway and the sickroom, close enough to seem neutral. "But being there isn't the same as telling it straight," Colton said. "My grandmother was at my uncle's wedding and told my aunt a version of it that started a fight that lasted three years." Khloe laughed, then stopped laughing, because they both knew families like that.

He wrote the essay Thursday night. It argued that a reader had to hold two positions at once, trusting Nelly enough to follow the story and doubting her enough to check her, and that the book seemed to know this about itself. He wrote a paragraph admitting that he could not fully separate what Heathcliff did from what Nelly wanted readers to believe he did, and that the gap might be the whole point or might be nothing, and he left the gap open on purpose. It was the first paper he'd handed in all year without a concluding sentence that pretended certainty.

When Ms. Pierre returned it Monday, she had written one comment in the margin in green ink: "Now read your own first paragraph the way you read Nelly." Colton read the paragraph again in the hallway, leaning against the lockers, and found that he did not entirely trust the boy who had written it, the one who claimed he had simply been too busy to notice the narrators until Thursday.

"Is that a bad thing?" Khloe asked, reading over his shoulder.

"I don't know." He folded the paper and put it in his backpack, between a permission slip and half a granola bar. "Ask Lockwood."

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: Some leases require the tenant to carry renter's insurance, which covers the tenant's own belongings rather than the building and adds a monthly premium.
story:
The laundromat on Fell Street smelled like warm lint and someone else's detergent, and Liam had spread two apartment leases across the folding table like a general surveying a map of territory he could not quite afford. His mother's ancient sleeping bag churned in the dryer behind him, a payment of sorts for her letting him use the evening to do this, when he was supposed to be doing the family's laundry. He had a pencil, a calculator app, and the growing suspicion that both apartments were lying to him.

The first unit, a studio near campus, advertised nine hundred a month. The second, a shared two-bedroom out past the bridge, listed at seven-fifty, which was why Adriana kept texting him that he'd be an idiot to pay more for less. But the numbers would not stay still. The studio included water but not electricity. The two-bedroom split all utilities three ways with a roommate he had never met. Every time Liam thought he had a total, another line item crawled out of the lease and changed it.

Adriana pushed through the door with a duffel bag of soccer jerseys and dropped it on a washer with the ceremony of someone burying a rival. "Please tell me you've decided," she said. "Because I've decided for you, and you're taking the cheap one, and I'm visiting constantly."

"Look at this first." He slid the studio's lease across the table and tapped a clause on page six, fine print he had nearly skipped, the kind of paragraph that exists to be skipped. It required the tenant to carry renter's insurance.

"What's that even cover?" Adriana frowned at it, thumbs hooked in the pockets of her hoodie.

"My stuff, apparently. Like if my laptop gets stolen or the ceiling leaks on my books. Not the building. The building's the landlord's problem." He said it and then checked it against the clause again, because it sounded too reasonable to be buried on page six. The clause even gave a minimum coverage amount, which meant a monthly premium, which meant his nine hundred had quietly become something else.

He remembered then, the way you remember a debt, sitting in Ms. Martínez's classroom junior year while she taught them to read contracts before signing them. She had handed out a gym membership agreement full of cancellation fees and made them find every one, and the boy next to Liam had found a fee even she'd missed, and she had grinned and said, "See? The fine print rewards the paranoid." He had thought it was the least useful hour of his life. Now he was that paranoid boy, in a laundromat, and he felt an obscure gratitude that curdled slightly into resentment, because knowing what to look for didn't make looking any cheaper.

The quote came up on his phone, twelve dollars a month from a company whose mascot was a cartoon umbrella. He typed it in. Nine twelve. Then electricity, maybe sixty, since water was included. He wrote nine seventy-two and underlined it, twice, the pencil pressing hard enough to dent the paper. "So the studio's nine seventy-two," he said. "All in. Every month."

Adriana had pulled a jersey from her duffel to inspect a grass stain and now held it up like evidence in a trial. "And the cheap one?"

"Seven-fifty, plus utilities split three ways, so maybe forty each, call it seven ninety." He paused, because here was the part he did not want to say. "Except I haven't read that whole lease yet. Page six of this one had insurance hiding in it. What's hiding in theirs?"

"Then read it," she said, and stuffed the jersey into the washer, and added, with the air of a person settling a matter, "I could read the pages you've already done. Two perspectives. Instantiate the division of labor."

"You just want to use that word in a sentence."

"I've been saving it." She sat down across from him and pulled the second lease toward her, and for a while there was no talking, just the thunder of the dryer and the tick of her pen against the table, which meant she'd found something and was deciding how he'd take it. "Li," she said finally. "Theirs requires it too. Same thing, page nine. Renter's insurance."

He took the lease from her and read it himself, because trusting her summary felt different from knowing, and there it was. He added twelve to the two-bedroom's column. Eight-oh-two versus nine seventy-two. A hundred and seventy dollars a month apart, still, but a hundred and seventy that had not existed twenty minutes ago, and he had the sudden vertiginous sense that every price he'd ever been told was only the opening bid of a longer conversation.

"Is any of this even germane?" Adriana asked, waving at the clauses. "Like, does it matter which one, if they both do it?"

"It matters because now I know the number's real," Liam said. "Before, I was comparing two things I'd made up." He looked at his columns, at the gap that had survived but changed shape, and then at the sleeping bag still tumbling, its orange fabric lit through the dryer window like a slow small fire. He took out his phone and opened the text to his mother, the one that said he was choosing the cheap one, and deleted it.

Behind them, the dryer buzzed, done.

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: In Classical-era sonata-form movements, the exposition is often marked with repeat signs, so the performer plays it twice before the development begins.
story:
Naomi had been listening to the same forty seconds of Mozart for twenty minutes, and Yousef had finally had enough of it. They were in the back room of the community centre, where the folding tables smelled of floor cleaner and somebody's yoga class had just emptied out down the hall. Ms. Lombardi had left the score on the piano stand with three coloured pencils and a note that said only, "Mark what you hear, not what you think you should hear."

"Okay," Yousef said, sliding his chair back from the table. "I'm going to say something and you're not going to like it."

"Say it."

"The pianist messed up." He tapped the counter of the old boombox they were using because neither of their phones could survive a whole afternoon on one charge. "Right here. He's playing along, it's going somewhere, and then he just starts over. Like he lost his place."

Naomi rewound the tape. She had heard it too, the first time through, that flicker of doubt before the return, and she had let it pass because she wanted the piece to be a straight line, a story that only moved forward. She listened again with her eyes shut. The music arrived at a kind of settling, a pause with two dots and a thick line staring up at her from the page, and then it did begin again, note for note, from the beginning.

"It's not a mistake," she said, mostly to herself.

"It literally is. He goes back to bar one."

She pulled the score toward her and ran her finger along the repeat signs, the paired dots that folded the music back on itself. "In these movements the exposition has repeat signs," she said. "The player plays it twice before the development starts. It's written in." Even as she said it, she felt the small vertigo of it, that a form could include its own doubling, that the second time through was the same and also not the same, because she was different now, waiting for what came after.

Yousef squinted at the page the way he squinted at her chess games, which he considered garrulous, all that talking between moves. "So the pianist knew he was doing it."

"He had to."

They marked the exposition in blue, the moment Yousef had called the mistake turning out to be its far border. Ilan arrived halfway through with a bag of clementines and the energy of someone who had walked the whole way in the rain, and he promptly took the opposing view, which was his custom and, Naomi privately thought, his gift. "Twice the same thing is boring," he said, peeling a clementine in one long spiral. "The composer should have cut it."

"That's a bromide," Naomi said. "Musical bromide. Anything repeated is redundant if you don't bother to listen for what changed."

"Nothing changed. Same notes."

"The listener changed."

Ilan pointed a segment of fruit at her. "That's the kind of thing Ms. Lombardi says."

"She'd operationalize it, though. She'd make me prove it." Naomi took the blue pencil back out and, in the margin of the second pass through the exposition, wrote nothing, then wrote "same, but I was waiting," then felt embarrassed and crossed out the second half so only "same" remained. The crossed-out part was still legible. She decided she could live with that.

The rain got harder against the window, and the room went the grey of late afternoon pretending to be evening. They worked through the development section together, the three of them arguing about where the music stopped being the first theme and started being its own dismantling, and Naomi found that her instinct was to want borders, clean ones, while Yousef wanted the seams to stay open and Ilan wanted to argue about it forever. She drew the borders anyway, in blue and then, uncertainly, in green, and understood that the colours were less a map than a set of guesses she would have to answer for on Thursday.

When they got to the recapitulation, the first theme came back whole, and Ilan, who had been slouching, sat up straight. "Okay," he said. "That part I like. It comes home."

"Everything comes home eventually," Yousef said. "The question is what it costs to get back."

Naomi looked at the page, at the exposition marked twice, at the crossing-out she had not fully committed to. She thought about telling them that she had liked it better when she thought the pianist had made a mistake, that errors had a human shape the score lacked, but the thought felt like something to keep for the walk home. She closed the score and squared the pencils against its edge.

"Same time Thursday," she said, and turned off the boombox while the rain kept on against the glass.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: Elgar took the title Pomp and Circumstance from Shakespeare's Othello, which mentions the "pride, pomp, and circumstance of glorious war."
story:
The party had spilled from Puneet's kitchen into the backyard, where folding chairs leaned against the fence and someone's younger brother was collecting abandoned plastic cups in a laundry basket. Mathis stood near the cooler with his gown still half on, the sleeves tied around his waist like an apron, and watched Puneet connect his phone to the speakers on the porch. The first chords of Pomp and Circumstance rolled out over the grass, and half the yard groaned while the other half laughed, and Puneet held the phone above his head like a trophy.

"We walked to this an hour ago," Nellie said, coming over with two paper cups of lemonade. "You're punishing us with it now?"

"I'm honoring us," Puneet said. He turned the volume down one notch when a neighbor's window opened across the alley. "Also I want to know something. Why is it called that? Pomp and Circumstance. What does that even mean?"

Mathis took the second cup from Nellie and drank before he answered, because something was assembling itself in the back of his mind, the way a word you half know drifts up when you stop chasing it. He had sat through a semester of Othello with Mr. Oliveira, and Mr. Oliveira had a habit of making them find the source of every phrase that had outlived its play. "It's Shakespeare," he said. "It's from Othello. The pride, pomp, and circumstance of glorious war."

Nellie frowned into her cup. "You mean we walked in to a war quote?"

"That's the phrase Elgar took the title from," Mathis said. "That's where the name comes from." He could see the line on the page, could almost hear Mr. Oliveira reading it, and he did not add the part he wasn't sure of, which was whether Elgar had meant it straight or meant it as a kind of ache, the glory being the thing Othello was losing. He suspected Mr. Oliveira would say the second and then refuse to commit to it himself, which had always struck Mathis as a dodge until tonight, when it was starting to feel like honesty.

Nellie tried to preempt his next sentence and failed, starting "So basically" and then stopping, because there was no basically. Puneet sat down on the porch step. "I walked across a stage to that music thinking it was about, like, achievement. Not war."

"Maybe it's both," Mathis said. "Maybe it's synecdoche, the way Mr. Oliveira would say. The music stands in for the whole thing." He gestured at the gown knotted around his waist, the chairs, the laundry basket of cups. "Like how this becomes graduation in your head, instead of just a hot afternoon in Puneet's yard." Nellie looked at him for a long second, then said that was the most he'd said all night, and Puneet said it was the most anyone had said about the music, ever.

The screen door opened and Mr. Oliveira came out carrying a plate of cookies he had apparently been deputized to deliver. He was a neighbor of Puneet's family, which was the only reason a teacher was at the party, and Mathis felt a small panic, the kind you feel when a private thought walks into the room in a cardigan. Mr. Oliveira had heard the whole exchange through the door, he admitted, or most of it, and he wanted to know which of them had caught the Othello line on their own. Puneet pointed at Mathis. "And does he have it right?"

"He has the source right," Mr. Oliveira said, which was exactly the noncommittal move Mathis had predicted, and which somehow satisfied him completely.

Later, when the sky had gone the color of a bruised plum and the music had moved on to something Puneet's mother had chosen, Mathis found himself at the fence with his father, who had arrived late from work and still had his ID badge clipped to his shirt pocket. His father talked about how proud he was, and about his own father, and about how he'd been the first in his family to finish anything, and how there had been years when they were nearly indigent and graduation had seemed like a rumor from another country. Mathis listened and did not translate the afternoon for him, did not mention war or Shakespeare or music borrowed from a tragedy. He understood that his father heard triumph in those chords and he himself heard something more complicated, and that both could be true at once, and that he would need a long time, probably years, to say what the uncertainty actually contained.

His father asked if he was tired. Mathis said a little. His father nodded toward the yard, where Nellie was teaching Puneet's little brother a clapping game and losing on purpose, and said they could stay ten more minutes. Mathis untied the gown from his waist, folded it over the fence rail, and went to get his friend another lemonade.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: The word blocking comes from 19th-century directors such as W. S. Gilbert, who planned scenes on a model stage using a block for each actor.
story:
The rehearsal room smelled of dust and radiator paint, and Mya spread the stage floor plan across two pushed-together desks like a map of a country she was supposed to govern by Friday. She had volunteered to direct the one-act before she understood what directing meant. Now she understood it meant standing in front of Paulina and Antonin with a pencil and telling them where to go, and they would either go or they would argue, and both possibilities frightened her in different ways.

She had tried running it like a drill. On Tuesday she had called out moves like a coach, crossing stage left, downstage right, and Antonin had shuffled where told but delivered his lines to the wall, flat as a taped announcement. On Wednesday she had tried the opposite, asking them where they thought they ought to stand, and they had stood wherever they pleased and the scene had gone soft, shapeless, two people talking in a room rather than two characters colliding. The two methods sat in her notebook like rival governments, and she could not get them to share power.

That night she was scrolling for anything, some third way, when she found a paragraph about W. S. Gilbert, the man who wrote the comic operas. "That's where blocking comes from," she told Paulina the next morning, before first bell, holding her phone between them in the crepuscular light of the gym hallway. "Nineteenth-century directors like Gilbert planned whole scenes on a model stage, and they used a block for each actor. That's the word. Blocking." Paulina looked at her the way she looked at crossword clues, half annoyed, half interested.

"It's just where we stand," Paulina said.

"It's why we stand there," Mya said, though she wasn't certain she could defend that yet.

At lunch she claimed a corner table and emptied her coin purse across it: quarters for the principal roles, nickels for the smaller ones, a dime she decided would be the chair. She slid them through an imaginary doorway, watched them avoid each other, converge, retreat. It was strange how quickly the coins stopped being money and started being people. When the quarter playing Paulina's character turned away too early, Mya saw the problem instantly, the moment her own voice in rehearsal had papered over: the character should want to stay. She moved the coin three inches and the scene, in her head, changed temperature.

She tried it again after school with the actual actors, kneeling on the stage with Mr. Lee's battered model platform, a dusty rectangle of plywood he kept in the props closet and let her borrow without asking what for. She set down two erasers from the chalk tray. "Antonin, you enter here, you're at the window by her line. Paulina, don't turn around until he says her name." It was still direction, still her deciding, but it stopped being command and became something like evidence. She could show them the shape of the argument before asking them to perform it, and they could argue with the erasers instead of with her, which, it turned out, they much preferred doing.

"That's better," Antonin admitted, after running the scene twice. "But it feels like you're playing both of us."

"I am a little," Mya said. "Tell me where I'm wrong."

Paulina crouched beside the platform and nudged the eraser. "She wouldn't come this close yet. She'd make him come to her. She's been waiting all play to make him come to her." Mya wrote it down, the coin logic and the actor logic meeting in the middle of the page, and felt something click that she could not yet have explained to anyone, a place where planning and listening turned out not to be opposites at all but two halves of the same attention.

Friday afternoon, Mr. Lee sat in the third row of the darkened house while they ran the act straight through, and Mya stood in the aisle with her notebook, calling only two stops. Once for a missed light cue, once because Antonin had drifted into the exact spot where Paulina needed to pass, a collision the erasers had predicted and his body had forgotten. Afterward Mr. Lee said the staging had a point of view, which was the most he ever said about anything, and Mya held on to the words the whole walk to her locker.

She still didn't know whether she was a director or just a girl who had found one good trick with coins, and she could not exculpate herself from Tuesday, the day she had treated her friends like equipment. Maybe some of that would always be in the room with her. But the coin purse was in her backpack, and next term there was a winter showcase, and she caught herself already assigning parts of the cafeteria tabletop to imaginary quarters, one hand flat on the formica like a stage.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: Australia has used compulsory voting in federal elections since 1925, and people who do not vote without a valid reason can be fined.
story:
The registration form had been sitting in Claire's binder for two weeks, folded once against a pencil sharpener, and she took it out again during fifth period while Mr. Andersen wrote discussion questions on the board. Her birthday was in March. The municipal election was in April. For the first time in her life, the timing lined up, and the fact of it kept surfacing at odd moments, like a coin she kept finding in her coat pocket.

"Are you actually going to vote for the school board?" Boston asked, leaning across the aisle. "Nobody votes for the school board."

"That's kind of the point," Claire said. "Turnout was, like, eleven percent last time."

Mr. Andersen turned around. "Since we're all so interested in local democracy," he said, dry enough that Claire suspected he had engineered the whole seating chart, "let's compare systems. Australia. Somebody tell me something about voting in Australia."

Youssef, who kept a running file of strange facts on his phone, was already scrolling. "Okay, wait," he said. "It says here Australia has used compulsory voting in federal elections since 1925. Compulsory. You have to vote." He looked up. "And people who don't vote without a valid reason can be fined. Actually fined."

"That can't be right," Boston said.

"Scrolling. It's right. It's a fine, like a parking ticket."

The room got loud fast. Claire didn't say anything at first. She was turning the fact over the way she turned over a proof in geometry, testing whether it held its shape. A fine for not voting. It struck her as both obvious and bizarre: obvious because of course turnout would be a problem otherwise, bizarre because the whole thing she'd been raised on was that voting was a choice, a freedom, the thing people marched for. Nobody marched to be compelled.

"Coerced voting isn't free voting," Boston said, when Mr. Andersen made them organize into sides. "If you have to do it, the act means less. It's like, if your parents make you apologize, the apology doesn't count."

"But the result counts," Youssef said. "Whoever wins, wins with everybody included, not just the people who care enough to be loud."

Claire found herself sitting in the middle of the room, literally and otherwise. She had come into class that morning with an incipient sense of her own position, mostly inherited from her mother, who believed that low turnout was a civic embarrassment and that people who skipped elections had forfeited their right to complain. But her mother's certainty had always sat uneasily next to something Claire couldn't quite name until now: a suspicion that being told what your duty was could desensitize you to it, the way fire drills made fires feel like a chance to stand outside.

Mr. Andersen refused to referee. "Claire," he said, because of course he did, "you've been quiet."

"I'm trying to figure out whether the fine changes what voting is," she said slowly. "Like, is a vote you're forced to cast the same object as a vote you choose to cast? Is it still speech if it's mandatory?"

"Or is attendance mandatory and speech still free?" Youssef offered. "You show up, you can spoil the ballot, but you showed up."

"Then the fine is only for the showing up part," Claire said, and felt something click. "That's actually different from what I thought we were arguing about."

That night she sat at the kitchen table with the registration form and her laptop open, and she asked her mother directly whether she'd ever skipped an election. Her mother rinsed a glass for a long time. "Once," she said. "Nineteen ninety-eight. I was twenty-three and I thought neither candidate would change anything for me." She set the glass down. "I was wrong about that, but not in the way you'd want me to say."

Claire thought about that. Her mother's generation treating voting as optional, then lecturing about it later, versus a country that had decided in 1925 to remove the option entirely. Neither arrangement felt like the whole answer. What she kept circling back to was Boston's argument about meaning and Youssef's about results, and the strange possibility that they weren't actually opposed: that a system could compel the habit and still leave the meaning to each person who walked in.

She mailed the form the next morning before first bell, standing at the blue box outside the post office in a wind that kept lifting the envelope's flap. In class, Mr. Andersen asked if anyone had changed their position since Tuesday. Boston raised his hand, which surprised Claire, since Boston never admitted movement.

"I still think forcing people is wrong," Boston said. "But I looked it up, and basically everyone shows up there, and I couldn't figure out who in Australia is being harmed. So I might be wrong about the harm part."

"That's all I ask," Mr. Andersen said. "Not that you change your mind. That you can say the word might."

Clarence wrote nothing down. She was watching the light move across the whiteboard and thinking that in April she would walk into a gymnasium, probably the one where she'd had PE since sophomore year, and cast a vote nobody had fined her for or compelled, and that the freedom would feel different now that she knew it could be otherwise. Or it would feel the same, and she'd spend the walk home wondering which was true.

"Still undecided?" Youssef asked, catching her in the hall after the bell.

"About the school board? Completely."

"Good," Youssef said. "That means you're taking it seriously."

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Claude Monet painted more than thirty views of the facade of Rouen Cathedral in 1892 and 1893, showing it under different light at different times of day and year.
story:
I was not worried about the portfolio, which is what I told everyone, and mostly what I believed. Ten pieces, one theme, an artist's statement by June. Ms. Harper had assigned it in September, and by October I had two paintings of the sycamore behind the gym, one at dawn and one at dusk, and I had decided this was a strong start rather than a thin one.

"You keep saying strong start," Rayane said on the bus to the gallery. She had her headphones around her neck like a collar. "You've said it four times."

"I said it twice."

"Twice this morning. Yesterday you said it was a foundation." She looked out the window at the warehouses along the canal. "Abel thinks you're stuck."

Abel, two rows back, was drawing in his sketchbook, so he couldn't be blamed for the opinion, though I blamed him a little anyway. I wasn't stuck. I was deliberating. Those were different things, and I resented that nobody in my life seemed to know the difference.

The gallery was cool and dim, the way galleries are, with benches in the middle of each room like the rooms expected you to sit down and be changed by something. Ms. Harper gave us a sheet of questions and released us. I answered the first two about composition and light without much interest, and then I turned a corner into a long room hung with paintings of the same building, over and over, a stone church front rendered in pinks and greys and a strange acid yellow, and I stopped walking.

Rayane caught up to me and read the wall text out loud, slowly, the way she read when she didn't believe a sentence. "Claude Monet painted more than thirty views of the facade of Rouen Cathedral in 1892 and 1893, showing it under different light at different times of day and year." She looked at the paintings, then at me. "More than thirty. Of one wall."

"One facade," I said, and my voice did something I hadn't authorized. I walked down the row. The stone was blue in one, almost white in another, orange as a coal in a third, and it was the same stone, the same doors, the same sculpted saints standing in their niches like an obdurate jury, unchanged while the light made each painting a different painting. I had assumed, before that room, that variety meant variety of subject. It had not occurred to me that a single subject could be the theme rather than the limitation, that the differences lived in a stratum I hadn't been looking at, in what happened to a fixed thing.

I sat on the bench to preempt the feeling arriving any harder than I could manage standing up. It wasn't panic. I want to be clear that it wasn't panic, even though Rayane came over and sat down and said, "You're doing your stuck face," and even though my eyes were doing something inconvenient. I said I was fine. I said I had known this already, that this was what I'd been doing with the sycamore, which was a lie of the sort I tell fluently, the kind that becomes half true through repetition.

But here is the honest part, the part I didn't say to Rayane on the bench and didn't say to Abel when he found us and stood with his hands in his pockets looking at the yellow cathedral: Monet's paintings were good, and mine weren't yet, and the idea alone wouldn't fix that. He had painted more than thirty because the first ones must have failed him, because light refuses to cooperate, because a thing seen at six in the morning in March is not the same thing at all. I had two paintings. To make ten of that tree would take the whole winter, dawn after dawn, and I could not promise the tenth would be better than the second. That stayed uncertain. I let it stay uncertain.

On the bus home I took out my notebook and wrote at the top of a clean page, One tree, ten mornings, and underneath, in smaller letters, like a confession I could still deny: possibly a bad idea. Abel leaned over the seat and read it.

"Possible bad ideas are still ideas," he said.

"Strong start," I said, and this time I laughed, and started a list: sunrise, fog, rain, the day the leaves come, the day they go.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Compound or coating chocolate, which replaces some or all cocoa butter with other fats, sets without tempering but does not have the same snap.
story:
The thermometer read 118 degrees and Edouard's mother still had not come home from the hospital, where his grandmother had been since Tuesday. He had chosen this evening for the chocolate because Ms. Ramos had said, on the last day of culinary club before spring break, that tempering wanted your whole attention. She had said it almost as a warning. So he spread the parchment across the counter, chopped the bar of dark couverture into pieces the size of fingernails, and set the steel bowl over the pot of barely simmering water, and decided not to think about the hospital at all.

The first attempt failed. He had been too careful, actually, moving the chocolate like a man defusing something, and when he spread a test smear on the parchment it dried dull and streaked, bending instead of snapping when he bent it. The seed method was supposed to save him: melt two-thirds, pull it off the heat, drop in the reserved third, stir until the crystals formed and the temperature slid toward 88. He understood the theory. He had watched four videos twice each. But theory was a sycophant, he thought, telling you that you already understood when you had only admired, and admiration was not the same as the burnt smell now rising because he had let the bowl touch the water.

He started over with the last of the good chocolate. While it melted he texted Anabelle, because she had spent the summer at her cousin's campsite and had once, over cafeteria fries, described making candy in a paper cup. Did your candy melts snap, he typed, like when you broke them. She wrote back in fragments, the way she always did when she was supposed to be studying. No tempering, she said. We just melted them and they set fine. Dipped pretzels. Shiny-ish. He stared at that for a while. His own chocolate needed this whole ceremony of temperatures and seeding, and hers had set in the woods with nothing.

He called her. "That's the difference," Anabelle said, before he had even finished the question, because she had looked it up after the campsite, having wondered the same thing at midnight in July. "Those are compound or coating chocolate. They replace some or all of the cocoa butter with other fats, so they set without tempering." She paused, and he could hear her roommate's music behind her. "But they don't have the same snap. That's the trade. Easy, or good."

He thanked her and hung up and stood at the counter with his phone in one hand and the spatula in the other, and he could not stop thinking that this was a metaphor for something, though every version he tried felt tangential, clever on the surface and beside the point underneath. The point was that his grandmother's surgery was scheduled for tomorrow morning and nobody had told him whether to come. His mother's texts had grown shorter all week, the way they did when she was protecting him, which he had been allowing because being protected was easier than being included.

He seeded the second batch. He stirred in figure eights, patient now, feeling the bowl's edge with his lip every thirty seconds the way the videos had shown, waiting for the moment when the chocolate thickened slightly and cooled toward 88. His phone buzzed on the counter. His mother: Coming home late. Don't wait up. He kept stirring. The test smear this time caught the overhead light and held it, a small dark mirror, and when he pushed a corner of it with the spatula an hour later it broke with a clean sound, like a knuckle cracking, and the break showed a matte satin edge instead of streaks.

He was so pleased that he photographed it, and then, because his hands were shaking slightly and he could admit that only now, in the privacy of success, he sat down on the kitchen floor with his back against the cabinet and made himself think the thing he had been desensitizing himself to all week with temperatures and videos: that tomorrow his grandmother might not be the same person, or might not be a person at all, and that no procedure of his, no careful seeding of attention, could guarantee an outcome. Some things you could temper. Some things only set, however they set, and you took them that way.

Then the phone buzzed again and it was not his mother. It was a number he half recognized, and the text said: It's Gran. Home by ten. Have you been eating? Set a plate for me. And beneath the astonishment of that, a smaller note from his mother followed thirty seconds later: Discharged early. Tests were wrong. Bringing her to you.

He got up off the floor. He took the tempered chocolate, still liquid in its bowl, holding its careful 88, and he poured a thin ribbon of it onto the parchment and dragged a fork through it so it set into a long ridged feather, the kind Ms. Ramos made for cake tops, because his grandmother had once said at some birthday that they looked like something from a palace. His hands were not entirely steady but the chocolate did not care, it did what it had been taught to do.

The door opened on his mother's voice and then a second voice, thinner than he remembered, saying, "Something smells burnt," and Edouard looked at the pan from the first batch, still soaking in the sink, and then at the shining feather hardening on the counter, and said, "That was practice. This one's the real thing." He snapped a corner off the test smear and held it out to her.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Psychologist George Bonanno's research on bereaved people found that resilience is common, and that there are no mandatory stages that everyone must pass through after a loss.
story:
The morning of the funeral, Anthony sat in the passenger seat of his father's car with the tie his grandmother had bought him folded in his lap, still in its plastic sleeve. They had to be at the church by eleven, and the drive from their house took forty minutes when traffic behaved, which on a Thursday it rarely did. His father drove with both hands on the wheel and the radio off, and neither of them had said anything since the driveway except that the coffee was on the counter and that Anthony should lock the front door.

Anthony had not cried yet. That was the problem he kept circling back to, the way a tongue returns to a loose tooth. His grandmother had died on Saturday, in a hospice room that smelled of lavender and hand sanitizer, and Anthony had held her hand and then gone home and slept nine hours. On Monday he had gone to school. On Tuesday he had laughed, actually laughed, at something Brayden said in the parking lot about the vending machine, a laugh so ordinary it had frightened him. He kept waiting for the wave everyone described, the crushing thing, and it had not come, and he had begun to wonder what was wrong with him, whether grief worked like a debt that accumulated interest.

"Maya texted," he said, when the silence got long enough to feel like a passenger between them. "She's saving us seats."

His father nodded. "That was decent of her." A tractor trailer merged in front of them, slow as a barge, and his father changed lanes without hurry, the turn signal ticking like a metronome.

Anthony opened his phone, not to answer Maya but because yesterday, unable to sleep, he had started searching things at two in the morning, typing questions into the dark. He had saved a page from his school's psychology database, something he'd found after skipping down a trail of links, and now he scrolled back to it and read it again. A psychologist named George Bonanno had studied bereaved people for years, following them through their losses, and had found that resilience was common. Not rare, not heroic, common. And there were no mandatory stages that everyone must pass through after a loss. No universal sequence. Anthony read the line three times while the guard posts of the highway fence ticked past the window, white, white, white.

"Find something?" his father asked.

"Kind of." Anthony turned the phone face-down on his knee. He wasn't ready to explain it, partly because explaining it felt like defending himself, like a lawyer pleading his own case, and how could he trust a verdict like that. "This guy studied people who lost someone. Most of them were okay. Like, functioning okay. And it wasn't because they skipped anything. There just wasn't a checklist."

His father was quiet through an overpass, long enough that Anthony thought the whole thing had landed wrong, had sounded like an excuse.

"When your grandfather died," his father said finally, "I went back to work in a week. My sister called me a month later, furious, said I hadn't grieved. Twenty years later she's still angry about it and I still don't know what she wanted from me." He adjusted the mirror a fraction, though nothing had changed behind them. "You looked at the etiology of grief at two in the morning? That's very you."

"I looked at everything. I couldn't figure out what was wrong with me." The fields outside the window were planted in low green rows, and a irrigation rig swung its slow silver arm across them like a clock hand. "Maya cried at school Monday and I just handed her a napkin. I felt like a fraud."

His father glanced over. "You took her to the vending machine."

"She wanted the pretzels."

"That's not nothing, Anthony." His father's voice stayed even, almost flat, and then it softened by one degree. "She was upset and you took care of her. There are worse ways to be broken."

Anthony looked at the tie in his lap, the plastic sleeve catching the light from the window. He had spent four days trying to diagnose himself, assembling a case history, and the whole time the evidence had been sitting in plain view: he had slept, eaten, gone to school, driven Maya to get pretzels because she couldn't eat the cafeteria food, let Brayden rant about the vending machine until the laugh came out of him. Maybe that was the thing itself, not the absence of it. He had wanted grief to arrive with a clear etiology, a cause he could trace and a course he could predict, and what he had instead was this, a Thursday morning, a tie, a church at eleven.

"It doesn't mean I won't fall apart later," he said, testing it out loud. "Like, I don't actually know that I'm resilient. I just know I'm not doing it wrong."

"Nobody knows that about themselves," his father said. "You do the day in front of you." He took the exit ramp, and the church appeared above the treeline, pale brick, the parking lot already filling with cars whose hoods gleamed in the sun. Maya was standing at the edge of the lot in a black dress and sneakers, waving with her whole arm. Anthony peeled the plastic off the tie and worked at the knot, getting it wrong twice while his father found a space between two sedans. Maya opened his door before he had finished.

"You're here," she said. "I saved the whole end of the pew." She looked at his crooked tie and reached up and fixed it without asking, her fingers quick and sure, and Anthony let her.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: In 2023, US workers aged 25 and over with a high school diploma had median weekly earnings of $899, compared with $708 for those without one.
story:
The hallway outside the gym smelled like floor wax and lukewarm coffee, and Hayden stood in it holding his gown over one arm because the gym itself had grown too loud, too full of relatives holding phones sideways. He had graduated an hour ago. The diploma was in a leatherette folder under his arm, and he kept shifting it, as if it might tell him something if he held it at the right angle.

Marie-Pier found him first. She still had her cap on, tilted, and she was carrying someone's baby, a cousin's probably, who gripped her honor cord with one determined fist. "My mother cried before they even read the names," she said. "Before. She heard the first violin note of the processional and she was gone." The baby yanked the cord and she let him. "Yours?"

"Making a speech in the parking lot, probably." Hayden meant his uncle. At the family dinner last night, between the second helping of his mother's rice and the store-bought cake, the uncle had leaned across the table with the air of a man delivering currency exchange rates. "You know what that piece of paper is worth?" he'd said. "In 2023, US workers twenty-five and over with a high school diploma had median weekly earnings of eight hundred ninety-nine dollars. Without one? Seven hundred and eight." He'd sat back, satisfied, as though he had personally arranged the hundred and ninety-one dollars.

Hayden had transcribed the numbers into his phone under the table, not because he doubted them but because he wanted to look at them later, alone, without the uncle's eyebrows hovering over them. He'd looked at them that morning while tying his shoes. Eight hundred ninety-nine. It was a strange way to learn what he'd done for four years was worth, in dollars, per week, in a country he didn't live in, to workers older than he'd ever been.

"There you are." Mikaella came down the hallway with her phone out, filming, apparently, the concept of hallway. "Mr. Kowalski's in the music room. He's cleaning out the cupboards. He says he wants to see you before you escape."

"I'm not escaping."

"Everyone's escaping. That's what graduation is." She lowered the phone. "Except him. He's staying. Thirty-one years in this building and he's finally retiring and he's spending his last hour alphabetizing sheet music."

Marie-Pier shifted the baby to her other hip. "You should go," she said. "You're the only one who ever actually talked to him."

Hayden went. The music room door was open, and Mr. Kowalski was on a step stool, sliding battered folders into a cardboard box, blowing dust off each one first like it mattered. He didn't turn around. "Choir or no choir, next year," he said, which was how he'd greeted Hayden for two years, ever since Hayden quit singing and started showing up anyway, sometimes, to sit in the back and do homework.

"No choir next year. No anything next year. I'm going to work for a year. Then maybe college."

Mr. Kowalski came down off the stool and looked at him properly. He had that way of making a pause do the work of a question.

"My uncle thinks the diploma's a paycheck," Hayden said. "He's got these numbers. Eight ninety-nine a week with it, seven oh-eight without." He hadn't meant to say it out loud, but the room was quiet and the numbers had been circling him all day like birds. "The thing is, he's not wrong. That's the annoying part. It's real money. But it's like he thinks that's the whole sentence and it's actually just the first clause."

"And the rest of the sentence?"

Hayden looked at the box of sheet music, at the cupboard standing open and emptied, at the thirty-one years of it going into cardboard. "I don't know yet. Maybe that it matters what I do with the rest of the week after the check clears. Maybe that's the part you can't transcribe into a table." He heard himself sound petulant and stopped, and Mr. Kowalski, who had heard four thousand teenagers sound petulant and worse, only nodded slowly, as though the sentence had arrived in acceptable condition.

"Sit," Mr. Kowalski said, and pulled out the piano bench. He opened the lid, not to play but to reach the pencils inside, and Hayden saw them: a decade of pencils, sharpened to different lengths, kept the way other men keep golf balls. "Take one. Every student I ever liked got one. It's not worth eight hundred ninety-nine dollars a week." He handed it over, short and toothless from use. "It's worth nothing. That's the point."

Hayden turned the pencil in his fingers and felt the evening tilt toward something both lighter and heavier, a small useless inheritance from a man who refused to price it.

Back in the hallway, Marie-Pier was waiting with the baby asleep on her shoulder and her cap finally off, hair flattened and wild at the same time. "Your uncle's looking for you," she said. "He wants a picture. He's holding your diploma folder and telling everyone at the vending machines about the eight ninety-nine."

Hayden pocketed the pencil and went to find him, and there the uncle was, beaming, folder raised like a trophy, and as Hayden got close the man opened it to display the certificate for the photo and found the inside empty, the paper still in the gym on the signing table, and stood there smiling at the camera with nothing in his hands but the cover.

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
knowledge_domain: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
fact: The United Kingdom's standard rate of VAT, a sales tax built into most prices, has been 20 percent since January 4, 2011.
story:
The paycheque came in a thin envelope with the Friday napkin order, and Noah slid it under the counter where the ketchup lived, because he already knew it would be wrong. He had counted the hours himself, nine shifts since the start of March, and the number in his head was not the number Ms. Joshi had written on the slip. He would open it after the dinner rush, when the register was quiet and he could think.

He bused tables through the crush, carrying the smell of onions and burnt butter with him like a second shirt. At table four a family spoke in accents he couldn't place, and when the father paid, he held up the credit card slip and frowned at it. "No tax line," he said to his wife. "Where's the tax on this?" Noah, stacking their plates, said it was on the menu prices already, that the thirteen percent was baked in. The man shook his head. "Back home it's VAT," he said. "Twenty percent, in the price." Noah filed that away, the way he filed the order for table nine, and kept moving.

When the family left, the father's printed copy of the bill stayed behind, folded once, smudged with sauce. Noah smoothed it out on the counter. A UK receipt, from a pub in York, kept in a wallet by habit maybe, used here as scrap paper for a note about train times. He couldn't read much from it, but he photographed it with his phone, because Karis had a thing about receipts and would want to see it.

At nine the rush thinned and he opened his envelope in the back hallway beside the mop sink. The paystub was denser than he expected. Gross pay, first, a number close to what he'd counted, and then a ladder of deductions descending from it: income tax, a chunk with no ceremony around it, then CPP and EI, acronyms he'd heard adults complain about without ever seeing them itemized. Below all of it, net pay, in bold. The bold number was short. Not robbed-short, he thought, but insulted-short, sixty-one dollars shorter than the hours he'd carried plates for. He put the slip in his pocket and did not look at it again until Abigale slid into a booth by the window with her backpack.

Abigale had driven over for the fries, which she called the only honest food in town, and for the argument, which she could expatiate on for half an hour without stopping. Tonight's subject was whether tips counted as wages, which she said was not a real question, just semantics. "A tip is a gift," she said. "A wage is what you're owed. Call it what you want, it's the same fries." Noah pulled out the paystub and the photo of the UK receipt and laid them side by side on the table like evidence. On the York receipt, nothing itemized; everything in the listed price. On his paystub, everything itemized, everything subtracted. Two systems with opposite instincts about what you were allowed to see.

"Twenty percent," Noah said, staring at the photo. "That's the UK rate. He said VAT's been twenty percent since January 4, 2011, and it's already in the prices, so nobody at the till ever sees it added." He'd looked it up on his phone during his break, thumbing through sites about rates and changes, and the date had been there, flat and certain. He didn't know yet what to do with it. It just sat next to the paystub like a second accusation.

Then Karis arrived, wet-haired from the swim pool, and leaned over the booth. She was the one who noticed things, the one who found the receipt interesting in the first place back when he'd texted her the photo, and now she picked up his paystub. He watched her eyes move down the columns, and he felt the floor of his certainty tilt. "These hours," she said, tapping the right side of the stub. "This column says year to date. That's everything since you started, not just this pay." He took it back. He counted the digits again, slower, and the missing sixty-one dollars dissolved, because it had never been missing; he had compared his March hours against a running total that stretched back to January, back before the cold snaps, back to his very first Sunday of scraping plates.

He had been ready, for most of an hour, to say something to Ms. Joshi at closing, something careful and rehearsed about accounting, and now he stood at the register with the folded stub in his fist and the sentence gone out of him. Suspicion, he thought, was endemic to anyone who'd ever been shortchanged, real or imagined; it spread through you whether or not there was anything to catch. Ms. Joshi came out of the kitchen untying her apron and saw him standing there. "Something wrong with the pay, Noah?" He put the stub flat on the counter between them, warm from his hand. "Could you show me how the deductions work," he said. "I want to know what I'm actually looking at."

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Skimming means reading quickly for the general idea, while scanning means searching a text for one specific detail such as a name or number.
story:
Parker had signed up for the language elective because it fit between chemistry and lunch, and only in the second week did he understand what it would demand of him: not vocabulary lists, but a short news article in Spanish, read aloud and summarized aloud, in front of everyone. Ms. Marino had taped a copy of the article to the classroom door, a piece about a river cleanup in a town he had never heard of, and she had said, in her unhurried way, that the summary was due Friday. Parker took a photograph of it with his phone and carried it home on the bus, where the light through the window made the screen look almost turbid, the ink of the print smudged by glare.

At his desk that evening he began at the first word and moved through the article one syllable at a time, translating as he went, writing each unfamiliar verb in the margin of his notebook. It took forty minutes to cover three sentences. He kept at it anyway, because that was how he had learned everything else, patiently and in order, and it had never failed him before.

By Thursday he had translated the entire article and could recite his English version nearly from memory, but when he tried to say it in Spanish, standing at his mirror with the door shut, the sentences collapsed. He knew every word and could not hold the shape of the piece in his head. He sat on the floor of his room with the article flat between his knees, tired in a way that felt older than the evening.

At school the next morning, Audrey-Ann watched him in the corridor outside the language room, hunched over the photocopy, lips moving. She had finished her own summary on Tuesday. "What are you doing?" she asked, and he told her, word by word, the whole thing. She looked at him for a moment the way people look at someone carrying a piano upstairs. "You don't need every word for a summary," she said. "You need the general idea. Read it fast, all of it, and don't stop at anything."

From where Audrey-Ann stood, Parker's face did something she recognized from physics class, the moment before a formula stopped being letters and became a shape. He turned back to the page and this time let his eyes run down it without pausing, ignoring the verbs he had spent three nights learning, letting the paragraphs blur into a single motion, and the article surfaced all at once, whole: a river, a cleanup, a town, an organizer, a promise. "That's it," he said quietly. "That's the general idea."

In the classroom, before Ms. Marino could call on anyone, Parker raised his hand. He read the first paragraph aloud, slowly but without stalling, and then set the page down and gave the summary in Spanish, his voice steadier than he expected, and when he stumbled on the word for volunteers, Violet, in the second row, mouthed it to him. Ms. Marino nodded and made a small note on her clipboard. Parker, still standing, found himself explaining what he had discovered, almost to the class and almost to himself. "Skimming is reading fast for the general idea," he said. "Scanning is different, it's hunting through a text for one specific detail, a name or a number. I was doing neither. I was reading everything and keeping nothing."

He was honest about the rest of it, too, because it seemed important not to pretend. "There's a date in there somewhere, for the next cleanup," he said. "I know I saw it. But I couldn't tell you what it is. I read past it every time." Ms. Marino considered him for a moment, then smiled in the way of someone who had planned the question before the semester started.

"Then that's your next task," she said. "Find it. But not by reading, Parker." She tapped her own copy of the article on the desk. "Find it the other way."

Parker looked down at the page, and there, four lines from the bottom, sat the date, bold and absurd, the one detail in the entire article he had never once stopped to see. Violet was already pointing at it.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: Braking distance is proportional to the square of speed, so doubling a car's speed makes the distance needed to brake about four times as long.
story:
The parking lot behind the shuttered grocery store had been empty for so long that weeds pressed up through the seams in the asphalt, and the painted lines had faded to the color of old bone. Arianna sat in the driver's seat with her hands at ten and two, exactly where Ms. Pierre had placed them, and tried to remember that the car was only a machine, that it had no opinions about her.

"Before we move," Ms. Pierre said from the passenger seat, "a question. If you double your speed, how much longer does it take you to stop? Twice as long? Take a guess."

"Twice," Arianna said. "That seemed obvious, but obvious answers had betrayed her before, on physics quizzes, on college applications, on the day she told her mother she didn't need a driving license in a city with buses. "Wait. Bruce had a problem set about this." She could picture him at the library table, chewing his pen, saying it half to himself. "Braking distance is proportional to the square of your speed. So if you double your speed, you need about four times the distance to stop."

Ms. Pierre smiled, which was not confirmation but permission. "Let's find out. Drive to that far line at ten miles an hour, then brake where I tell you."

Arianna eased the car forward. The lot was vast enough that ten felt like crawling, like the engine was atrophying under her foot, so slowly did the scuffed storefront drift nearer. At the line, Ms. Pierre said "Now," and Arianna pressed the brake, and the car stopped almost immediately, within a car length, so gently that her body barely leaned.

"Twenty this time. Same place to brake."

She accelerated. Twenty still felt like nothing, a bicycle's pace, and when Ms. Pierre said "Now," Arianna braked with the same pressure and the car kept going. It slid past the first stopping point, past the second, tires whispering on the gritty asphalt, and she did not stop the car until she had covered what looked like four of the lengths from before, all of them strung out in front of her like a sentence she had not meant to write. Her throat went tight. The storefront was still far away, and no one was hurt, and still her hands were shaking on the wheel.

"That's the square," Ms. Pierre said quietly. "Ten to twenty, and your stopping distance about quadrupled."

Arianna let out a breath. "I knew it on paper," she said. "I got it right on Bruce's quiz, actually. He let me copy check his answer and I told him he'd forgotten to square it." She laughed a little, unsteadily. "But knowing it and feeling it are different things. Knowing it is just words. Feeling it is, I don't know, affective. It's in your stomach." She had argued about this once with Tayden, who claimed that anything you could state in a sentence you therefore understood, and that the rest was sentiment dressed up as depth. She had called that sophistry at the time, showing off a word she'd found, and Tayden had laughed at her for it, and she had never decided who was right. Sitting here in the long skid mark of her own mistake, she thought they might both be right, in different ways, about different things, and that this was unsatisfying but probably true.

"Can we do it again?" she asked.

"Once more. Then we practice turns."

She drove back to the far line, the weeds nodding past the windows, and brought the car up to twenty again. This time she watched the asphalt unrolling toward her and thought of the square, the honest arithmetic of it, the way it did not care that twenty still felt slow. When Ms.ierre said "Now," she braked early and hard, and the car pulled up short of both the first mark and the second, well inside the distance she'd needed before.

"Better," Ms. Pierre said. "You're thinking ahead of the car now."

Arianna looked at the long black streaks she'd left on the faded lines, hers now, evidence. She put her hands back at ten and two and said, "Okay. Show me the turns."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: A pencil's core is a mix of graphite and clay; more clay makes a harder pencil with lighter marks, marked H, and less clay makes a softer, darker one, marked B.
story:
Lily had drawn the same river four times that morning, and each time the willows on the far bank had dissolved into grey clouds that spread across the paper like rumours. She sat cross-legged on the dock behind the craft cabin, a rubber eraser in one fist, rubbing at the smudge until the paper began to pill.

"That's the fourth one," Yousef said, dropping onto the plank beside her with his own sketchbook, already sweat-damp at the edges. The camp had assigned them both to the morning art block, and so far his strong suit was commentary. "What did you use, charcoal?"

"A pencil. Just a pencil." She held it up. The barrel read 6B, which she had chosen from the craft cabin's coffee tin because the marks had looked so rich and black when she tested it on scrap.

He took the pencil from her fingers and turned it in the light, then flipped open his book to show his own drawing of the same river, crisp and pale, every reed separate. "Mine's a 4H. I grabbed it because the letters made no sense, so I figured nothing mattered." He tapped her pencil's stamp. "Yours says B."

She remembered, then, the afternoon in March when her mother had taken her to the art shop on Division Street to buy supplies for her portfolio. She had stood at the pencil display for twenty minutes, picking up one after another and making little crescents on the tester pad taped to the counter, noticing without understanding that some crescents came out silver and some came out like bruises. The cashier had watched her with mild pity until her mother, checking her phone by the door, said they had to go. Lily had bought six of the softest ones because darkness had felt like seriousness.

Now she looked at her ruined willows, then at his clean reeds, and understood that something was happening that she had never bothered to codify: the cores of these pencils were not the same stuff in different moods. A pencil's core was graphite mixed with clay, she remembered the cashier saying at last, almost apologetically, as she bagged the six dark ones. More clay made a harder pencil that left lighter marks, and those were the ones marked H. Less clay made softer, darker ones, marked B. She had nodded and forgotten it in the parking lot.

"I used the wrong pencil," she said. Not to Yousef exactly, more to the river.

"For willows, maybe." He shrugged. "Or for hands."

But it was not that simple, and she knew it within the hour, because when she borrowed his 4H and tried to render the shadowed water under the dock, the pale strokes barely registered, and what she wanted there was weight, the kind of dark that her soft 6B gave up instantly and then betrayed her by traveling. She sat between the two failures and thought about Angela, who ran the camp's dining hall with the ruthless competence of a general and had told Lily last week that she hated art because art could not be graded. "Either the soup is seasoned or it isn't," Angela had said, ladling out the epicurean pleasure of a properly salted broth as though it were proof of an ordered universe. Lily had envied that. Now she envied it more.

Mr. Ong, who ran the craft cabin and was rumored to have failed out of architecture school twice, came down the dock at lunch with his thermos. He looked at her four smeared rivers laid in a row, said nothing for a long moment, and then bent and touched one smudge with a fingertip.

"Fixative would help," he said. "But the drawing underneath would still be wrong." He straightened. "Or right. Depends what you wanted."

"I wanted the willows to be soft," Lily said. "But not to bleed."

He looked at her the way the cashier had, but with less pity. "Then you have an interesting afternoon ahead of you."

She did not use fixative. Instead she started a fifth river, and this time she worked slowly, testing on scrap first: the 4H for the reeds and the far shoreline where she wanted air and distance, and the 6B saved for the under-dock dark, laid down once and then sealed under her open palm so it could not wander. She discovered she could not fully have both things, the softness and the control, and she did not pretend she had solved it. The willows came out sharper than she had wanted, the water darker, and the whole page held a compromise that nobody but her would recognize as one.

Yousef leaned over when she finished. "Better," he said. "That one you can actually look at."

She pinned it to the dock post anyway, facing the water, and sat back to see what the afternoon light would do to it. "Hand me the 4H again," she said. "I want to try the far bank once more."

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: On the practical driving test in Great Britain, parallel parking at the side of the road is one of the reversing manoeuvres the examiner may ask a candidate to do.
story:
The garage smelled of oil and cut grass, and Sienna had backed the family hatchback between Mr. Papadopoulos's wheelbarrow and his stacked plant pots eleven times before she admitted the truth to herself: she was good at bays and useless at kerbs. Her test was at nine the next morning. Between the car and the street she had one evening, two cones borrowed from the school gym, and Bronson leaning against the doorframe eating crisps.

"You've been practising bay parking for weeks," Bronson said. "Fancy bays. Nice straight lines. Like parking in a shopping centre."

"Because that's harder," Sienna said. "The angle's tighter."

Bronson crumpled the packet and dropped it in the bin Mr. Papadopoulos kept by the workbench, because Mrs. Papadopoulos checked. "My cousin failed twice. Both times the examiner made her park at the side of the road, between two cars. Parallel. On the practical driving test in Great Britain that's one of the reversing manoeuvres the examiner may ask you to do, and my cousin said they love asking it."

"Your cousin also said ghosts are real."

"Both things can be true."

Sienna sat on the garage step with her phone and looked it up, and Bronson was right, or at least the internet agreed with him. The examiner may ask for it. May. That single word sat in her chest all evening. She had planned everything cerebral and tidy, diagrams in a notebook, measurements, the kind of preparation that felt like erudition until the moment it met an actual kerb. Now the test had a door in it she hadn't practised opening.

Elissa arrived at seven with her own agenda, which she announced before she'd fully shut the gate. "If you pass tomorrow, you're driving us to the coast on Saturday. Bronson too. I've been planning it since March and my mum will not be driving us, she's made that clear." She set down her bag. "So. What's the crisis?"

"The crisis," Sienna said, "is cones," and she explained, and Elissa, who wanted the coast more than she wanted almost anything, became immediately and fiercely practical.

They set the cones in the road outside the garage to stand for the two cars, and Mr. Papadopoulos came out with his watering can and stayed to watch, which Sienna suspected he would do anyway, cats and neighbours being alike in that. The first attempt she mounted the kerb. The second she finished a metre from it, angled like a boat at a dock. She thought about the bay parking she knew, the geometry of it, the slow rotation of the wheel, and wondered whether the two things were really so different, or whether she'd only ever learned one prayer and pretended it was the whole religion.

"Stop thinking," Elissa called from the pavement.

"That's my whole personality."

"Then be someone else for ten minutes."

On the sixth try she brought the car in close, straight, within a hand's width of the kerb, and sat with her hands still on the wheel, breathing. Bronson whooped. Mr. Papadopoulos said, "Again," in the tone of a man who did not believe in single miracles, and she did it again, and then a third time in the dark, using only the mirrors.

She drove them out to the ring road for the merging, because the test route went that way and because Elissa had read the highway section aloud twice in the car like a lawyer with a closing argument. The slip road came up fast. Sienna checked the mirror, signalled, found her gap, and pushed in, and the lorry behind flashed its lights once, which she chose to read as forgiveness. Was that what confidence was, she wondered, deciding what other people's lights meant and acting on it anyway?

Back in the garage, headlights off, engine ticking as it cooled, she laid it out for them. "If he asks for a bay, I'm fine. If he asks for the side of the road, I'm probably fine now, probably. I don't know which one he'll pick, and I can't know, and I've decided that's allowed." She thought of the drive to the coast, Elissa's March plans, the cones still standing in the road like patient witnesses. "I can't expiate the last three weeks of practising the wrong thing. I can only parallel park at whatever side of the road I'm given."

Elissa hugged her. Bronson took the cones back to the gym bin under cover of dark, since technically he'd borrowed them for a "study group."

At eight fifty the next morning, in the test centre car park, the examiner clipped his board to the dash and said, "When you're ready, pull out, and then I'd like you to pull up on the right, then reverse two car lengths."

Sienna looked at him. "Not parallel?"

"Not today." He smiled slightly. "Drive on when you're ready."

She started the car, and something in her settled, not victory exactly, but the steadiness of a person who had practised for a door that never opened and was glad she'd opened it herself first.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex, published in 1949, contains the line usually translated as 'one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman', arguing that society shapes womanhood.
story:
The passage was taped to the kitchen table by Sunday afternoon, the paragraph from Jane Eyre where Jane agrees to marry Rochester, and Jaxon had written nothing underneath it except the word "lens" and then crossed that out. The essay was due first period Monday. He had until Olive and Klara arrived to figure out what a feminist lens actually was, other than a phrase Mr. Fortin had repeated three times on Friday with the patience of a man who knew half the class was pretending.

Olive arrived first, hauling her backpack onto the counter and stealing an apple without asking, which by now counted as asking. She leaned over his notebook. "You have one word and it's crossed out."

"I'm building suspense."

Klara came in through the back door a minute later, shaking rain off her jacket, and set down a bakery bag in front of Jaxon before he'd said anything. Half a cinnamon roll, still warm. She did that, noticed what people hadn't said they needed. "My mom bought two," she offered, which was not true, but Jaxon let it stand.

They spread out around the table. Olive read the passage aloud, her finger under the line where Jane says she will be Rochester's companion through life, and Jaxon heard it differently in a voice other than his own, heard the way the sentence gave everything away. "Okay," Klara said, "so the Marxist thing is easy. Jane's poor, Rochester owns the house, the marriage is also a transaction. Done. Five paragraphs."

"It can't just be done," Jaxon said. "Mr. Fortin said a lens has to change what you see, not just rename it." He was copying out the passage by hand, a habit that felt slower than typing but somehow made the sentences open up. "The feminist lens has to say something about Jane herself. Whether wanting him is her wanting him."

Olive pulled her laptop toward her. "My sister has this book," she said, typing. "The Second Sex. Simone de Beauvoir, 1949. She quoted it at me for like a month." She turned the screen so they both could see, and there was the line: one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman. Klara read it out loud, twice, the second time slower.

"So the argument is that society shapes womanhood," Olive said. "Whatever Jane thinks she wants, it's trained into her."

"She still wants it," Jaxon said. "That's the part that doesn't collapse." He wrote both sentences side by side in his notebook, the Beauvoir and the Jane, and looked at them until his eyes watered. "Maybe that's the essay. Not that the lens is right or wrong, but that both things are true at once and the book knows it."

"Mr. Fortin will call that hedging," Klara said. She had pulled the cinnamon roll apart and was pushing the larger half back toward Jaxon, which he pretended not to notice so she wouldn't take it back. "He maligns every essay that doesn't pick a side. Remember what he wrote on Dai's paper. 'A fence is not a position.'"

"He also said a good critic admits what stays uncertain," Jaxon said. "Same class. Same man." The clock above the stove said 8:40, and the 8:40 mattered now in a way the 8:00 before it hadn't; the essay was due in thirteen hours and he had a thesis and no paragraphs. Olive opened a blank document on her own laptop out of solidarity, or guilt, and began typing his outline while he talked, her fingers loud in the quiet kitchen.

He worked until eleven, the others gone, his mother leaving tea at his elbow without a word. In the third paragraph he wrote that Rochester's cosmopolitan worldliness, all his travels and his mistresses, was itself a kind of training, the privilege of having been allowed to become anyone at all, while Jane had been permitted exactly one shape. In the fifth paragraph he conceded that Charlotte Brontë might have intended none of this, that de Beauvoir wrote her line in 1949, nearly a century after the novel, and that a lens could illuminate a book the author never saw. He saved the file twice. Then he read the last sentence aloud to the empty kitchen, quietly, testing it: "One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman, and one is not born, but rather becomes, a reader, and both of us, Jane and I, are still mid-sentence." His mother's voice came down the hall, sleepy, telling him to go to bed, and he closed the laptop and sat for a moment with his hand flat on the warm cover, the way you'd steady something that might still move.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: 'I-messages', such as 'I felt stuck when the slides came in late', were promoted by psychologist Thomas Gordon in the 1960s as a way to raise problems without blaming.
story:
