The plan had been to rehearse the presentation at Justine's grandmother's house because the kitchen table was big enough for four laptops and the grandmother fed anyone who walked through the door. That part worked. What hadn't worked, according to the rubric Mr. Farah-Ali had handed back on Thursday, was the group process itself. "Your slides are lovely," he had written under Lance's name, "and your data is clean," under Kiefer's, "but you functioned as three soloists, not a team. Final practice before the real thing. Sort your feedback." Justine had been marked team lead, which meant the sorting was hers.

The problem was specific and it had a name, though she didn't say it out loud. Lance's slides arrived at eleven the night before every deadline, gorgeous and late, like a guest who shows up after the table is cleared. Justine had told him so, more or less, in the group chat: "we can't keep doing this." He had replied with a single thumbs-up, which was somehow worse than an argument.

Kiefer kicked her chair under the table. "Say it to his face. He's right there."

"I know where he is."

Lance looked up from his laptop. He was the sort of person who called himself an aesthete without irony and could spend forty minutes choosing between two nearly identical fonts. "Say what to my face?"

"Nothing yet," Justine said. "Eat your samosas."

The grandmother refilled the tea and then, without asking, cleared a stack of magazines from the sideboard and put down a book instead. "Your grandfather's," she said. "From when he taught. He kept everything." Justine reached for it mostly to be polite, and the spine cracked open to a chapter about running groups, about how to raise a problem without turning the other person into the problem. A paragraph near the top described a technique promoted by a psychologist named Thomas Gordon back in the 1960s, a way of phrasing complaints called an "I-message": instead of saying "you ruined it," you said something like "I felt stuck when the slides came in late." The blame drained out and the fact stayed in.

She read it twice. It looked almost too simple, like being told the cure for hiccups was a glass of water.

"Useful?" Kiefer leaned over her shoulder.

"Maybe." She copied the sentence onto the back of her chemistry notes and looked at it. "You ruined it" versus "I felt stuck when the slides came in late." The first was a wall, impermeable, nothing to do but stand behind it or knock it down. The second left a door.

The problem was that she didn't entirely believe it. She had watched her mother use soft language for years, smoothing every edge until nothing true survived the smoothing, and she suspected that "I felt stuck" could be just a coward's way of saying "you failed," dressed up in kindness. Lance wasn't stupid. He'd hear the accusation underneath.

So she tried it out on Kiefer first, quietly, while Lance was in the washroom. "Give me something annoying about my part."

"You talk too fast in the middle section and nobody can copy the figures down."

"Okay. If I say 'you're being inconsiderate when you speed up,' what happens?"

"I get defensive and say the figures are in the handout anyway."

"And if I say, 'I lose the room when I speed up, because I can't tell if they're following.'"

Kiefer considered. "Then I'd tell you to slow down and maybe put pauses in. Huh." He nudged the book with one finger. "That Gordon guy."

When Lance came back, Justine closed the chemistry notes, then opened them again, because pretending to be casual would be its own kind of lie. "I need to say something and I'm going to get it wrong, probably," she said. "Last cycle I felt stuck when the slides came in late, because I couldn't rehearse my section and I ended up sounding unprepared when that wasn't actually my fault." She held her breath. It felt like standing on a diving board.

Lance set down his fork. "You could have just said that in October."

"I said 'we can't keep doing this.'"

"That's a weather report. This is a weather report with coordinates." He pulled his laptop closer. "Eleven at night is when they look good, though. Earlier looks worse."

"I'd rather have worse and on time."

"Half as pretty," Kiefer offered. "Sixty percent."

"Forty percent pretty and I'll build you a template," Lance said. "You design the template, we fill it. Then everything matches and I don't spend an hour deciding between fonts."

Justine laughed, surprising herself. "That's the deal of the century."

They ran the full presentation twice, and the second time through, when Lance said "next slide" before Justine had finished her line, she caught his eye and said, "Hold. I felt rushed there, I want the number to land." He held. Nobody died. The grandmother brought dates and stood in the doorway listening with her arms crossed, and when they finished she said the part about supply chains was too fast, "like a radio announcer," and Lance said, "See, everyone's a critic," and Justine wrote it down anyway.

Walking to the bus stop afterward, Kiefer asked whether she'd use the Gordon thing for everything now, the roommate thing, the thing with her mother. Justine zipped her binder into her bag. "It worked tonight," she said. "Ask me again after something that matters." The bus came around the corner with its lights already on, and she ran for it.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Most news articles use the 'inverted pyramid': the most important facts come first and less important details follow, so the opening paragraph carries the core story.
story:
The festival had taken over the whole park by noon, and Henry had claimed a folding chair near the language pavilion, where a stack of newspapers sat beside a hand-lettered sign: LEIA EM PORTUGUÊS. His mother had signed him up for the exchange program in March, and the coordinator's email had been blunt. By the festival, you will read a short news article aloud and summarise it. No translations on your phone. His Portuguese was four months old and fragile, and the article he'd drawn from the stack was about a city council vote, dense with words he had never met.

He started where any careful person starts, at the beginning, but by the third sentence he was drowning. "Deliberação" stopped him, then "fundamento," then a clause that seemed to loop back on itself. He did what felt methodical: he flipped to the last paragraph, the shortest one, assuming it would be easiest, a ramp into the harder material. He spent ten minutes there, decoding a sentence about a spokesperson's schedule, and when he looked up, the page had told him nothing about the vote at all.

Heloise found him like that, pencil hovering over the final paragraph, his margins already crowded with guesses. "You're reading it backwards," she said. She was in his class, though he mostly knew her from the back of the room, where she translated for the Brazilian students whose parents worked at the university. She sat down without being asked and turned his paper right side up. "Start at the top. It's called the inverted pyramid. The most important facts come first, and the details follow, so the first paragraph carries the core story."

"That seems lazy," Henry said. "Hiding the conclusion at the top."

"Or honest. You can stop reading whenever you have enough." She tapped the opening paragraph. "Try it. Just this."

He worked through the first three sentences again, and this time they gave way, because they were built to. The council had rejected a plan to rename a street; the vote had been close; the mayor had called the proposal divisive. Everything after was explanation, history, a quotation from someone denigrating the council's deliberateness as cowardice. He'd been fighting through scaffolding when the building had been standing right there. Why had his teacher never mentioned this? Or had she, in October, while he was watching the clock? He wondered whether other things were arranged this way, whole subjects with their weight at the front, and he had been crawling in from the rear.

Abel arrived with two cups of something cold and took the chair on Henry's other side, reading over his shoulder with the entitlement of a longtime friend. "Summarise it to me," he said. "Out loud. You're performing at four."

Henry read the first paragraph aloud, his accent clumsy on the nasal vowels, and then set the paper down and tried to carry the sense without it. "The council voted against the new name. It was close. The mayor thinks the debate hurt the city." He stopped. "That's it, isn't it. That's the whole article in three sentences."

"You skipped the subpoena part," Abel said, pointing at a paragraph near the middle, where one council member had been ordered to testify about how the vote had been scheduled. "But it's not load-bearing. It's a detail."

"Then why is it in there?"

"Because newspapers are written for people who might get pulled away," Heloise said. "Like you, ten minutes ago."

Henry laughed, and it loosened something. He read the article a second time, then a third, marking which sentences could be lifted out without the story collapsing, and the structure revealed itself further: the second paragraph mattered more than the third, the third more than the fifth, a slope descending into quotations and calendar notes. His four o'clock slot was approaching. Ms. Rodríguez, who ran the pavilion and had graded his first stumbling attempts back in April, was setting out a microphone at the front, adjusting its height with the unhurried precision of someone who had done this many summers.

When his name was called, Henry stood, and on the walk to the microphone he noticed he was doing something new, sorting as he went, deciding what a listener needed first. He read the opening paragraph cleanly, better than he had all afternoon, and then looked up at the folding chairs, at Heloise and Abel and a row of Brazilian students he didn't know, and began without the paper: "The council voted no."

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: Mirrors leave blind spots beside and behind a car, so a quick look over the shoulder is needed before merging or changing lanes.
story:
The grocery store lot was half empty at eight on a Sunday morning, which was the only reason Madison's mother had agreed to it. Madison had already driven the loop behind the store twice, circling the loading dock, the cart corrals, the single faded cone she had placed between two painted lines to stand in for a parked car. Parallel parking, the driving test, Saturday. She backed toward the cone, turned the wheel, straightened, and opened her door to check the distance. Three feet. A mailbox could have fit in that gap.

"You're not even trying anymore," Elle said from the curb, where she sat with a bag of day-old donuts she'd bought inside as breakfast and entertainment. "You're just sort of leaning the car in the general direction of the cone."

"Lean is a technique," Madison said. She pulled forward and tried again, slower this time, watching the cone in her side mirror until it vanished at the rear bumper, then turning hard. The car slid in at an angle, rear tire kissing the curb. She got out, stood in the pale morning light, and looked at it. Better. Not good.

Elle came around to the passenger side with two donuts and handed one through the window. "So what happens if you fail?"

"Then I retake it, and my mom makes that face for another month." Madison took a bite. "The face is worse than the test."

At ten, her mother traded places with Timothy's older sister, who had agreed to take them onto the highway, since the test route ended with a merge onto Route 9 and Madison had never once done it at speed. The on-ramp came up faster than she expected. She checked the side mirror, saw nothing, and began to drift left toward the travel lane.

A horn, short and not angry, only announcing itself. A silver hatchback sat beside her, close enough that she could see the driver's coffee cup. Madison eased back into her lane, heart going like a drummer who had lost the tempo, and completed the merge behind the hatchback once it passed.

"Sorry," she said. "I looked. The mirror was empty."

"That's the trap," Timothy's sister said, not unkindly, keeping her eyes on the road. "Mirrors leave blind spots beside and behind the car. The look over your shoulder catches what they miss." She said it once, flat, like a fact she'd paid to learn, and then let the silence do the rest.

They drove five miles, took the next exit, looped back, and did it again. This time Madison turned her head, quick, chin toward the window, and there it was, a blue pickup sitting in the space her mirror insisted was empty. She stayed in the lane and merged behind it. On the third loop the shoulder check came without thinking, and on the fourth she caught herself doing it twice, almost showing off. The trick was not to stop trusting the mirror. The trick was to know what it couldn't tell her, which felt like something people should mention about more than mirrors.

Back at the grocery store, she parked between two actual cars, an old Buick and a pickup with a boat hitch, and the Buick's owner came out mid-maneuver, a small pugnacious man in a cardigan who stood with his hands on his hips as though preparing to impugn her entire generation. Madison finished the park, six inches from his bumper, and gave him a polite wave. He waved back, deflated by his own readiness, and drove away.

"He wanted to fight you," Elle said through the window. "You robbed him of it."

"He can have the donut hole." Madison held one out and Elle accepted her complicity in breakfast with a shrug, because she had encouraged the whole plan from the start, the lot, the cone, the highway loops, and knew it.

Her mother came out of the store with a cart and watched Madison pull out of the spot, re-approach, and back in again, once, twice, the second time leaving a foot of clearance, the third time closer. "Saturday," her mother said, loading the bags.

"Saturday," Madison said. She thought of the silver hatchback and the blue pickup, of all the cars that existed where the mirror said nothing did. She would look, and look again, and probably fail something anyway, though maybe not the parking. She turned the wheel, watched the cone's ghost where the Buick had been, and eased the car backward until the curb met the tire with a small, definite tap.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The first instant replay on television was shown by CBS during the Army-Navy football game on December 7, 1963, using a system devised by director Tony Verna.
story:
The stadium roared around Julia like something geological, a sedimentary noise built up over decades of Saturdays, and she felt it shift when the call went wrong. Navy's receiver had trapped the ball against his chest at the goal line, or hadn't; the official's arms went up for a touchdown while half the stands screamed that it hit the turf. Julia's father was on his feet beside her, shouting for a replay, and down the row Calder was holding his phone above his head, filming the jumbotron as though the stadium owed him evidence.

"They have to show it again," Mikayla said, leaning across Julia's brother to be heard. "They show everything again."

"They don't, though," Julia said. "Not here. Not live."

Her father turned around, incredulous. "It's a hundred million dollar facility. You're telling me they can't rewind a picture?"

Julia didn't answer, because she wasn't sure, and being unsure in her family was treated as a confession. She pulled out her phone, shielding the screen with her palm against the late-afternoon glare, and typed a question she half knew the answer to: when did they first replay a play on television. The results loaded slowly, throttled by forty thousand people in one bowl of steel, and while they spun she watched the field, where the official was conferring with another, hands circling each other like a man trying to circumscribe the truth with his fingers.

The article came up. She read it twice, then a third time, because the specificity of it seemed too precise for a day this chaotic. The first instant replay on television had been shown by CBS, during the Army-Navy football game, on December 7, 1963. A director named Tony Verna had devised the system. She sat with that for a moment. An Army-Navy game, of all things, the same match her grandfather used to watch, and a man in a production truck who had figured out how to fold time backward for an audience. She thought of Verna's crew rolling the tape and the crowd at home believing, for a few seconds, that they were watching the play happen again rather than a ghost of it, and she wondered whether that first audience had known the difference.

"Found it," she said aloud. "The first instant replay on TV. CBS, Army-Navy game, December 7, 1963. A director named Tony Verna devised the whole system."

"So it exists," her father said. "So they can do it."

"That was television," Julia said. "That's the thing. It was a broadcast thing, for people at home. The people in the stadium in 1963, they just saw whatever they saw." She could feel the shape of an argument forming, and she was careful with it, because Calder would test it. "The replay was never for the crowd. It was for the camera's crowd."

Calder lowered his phone. "So we're the crowd. We're the ones replays were never for."

"Reviews are different," Mikayla said. "The booth reviews. They have that now."

"They have it, and we don't get to see it," Calder said. "The referee goes under the hood and the rest of us stand here in the dark deciding whether to be angry."

Julia looked down at the field, where the officials had finished conferring. The touchdown stood. Her father sat down hard, muttering about culpability, about how a man in a striped shirt could cost Navy the game and never have to answer for it, and the word snagged in Julia's mind because it cut both ways. The official might have cost them the game. But so might the receiver who bobbled it, the cornerback who arrived a half step late, the entire sedimentary weight of every decision that had deposited them all into these seats on this particular Saturday. Assigning blame was easy. Circumscribing it, drawing the line around who was actually responsible for one trapped ball in a game with a hundred moving parts, was something no camera could do.

"The crazy thing," she said quietly, mostly to Mikayla, "is that in 1963 people at home saw the replay and some of them thought it was a second play. A fumble or something, happening live. They didn't know what they were looking at."

Mikayla laughed, a short, surprised sound. "So even when you show people the truth, they don't recognize it."

Julia nodded slowly, watching the teams line up for the extra point. She still didn't know if the receiver caught it. Neither did her father, or Calder, or the man in stripes, probably, not really. Somewhere above them the cameras had it all on tape, absolute and indifferent, and none of them would ever see it. "I don't know if that makes me feel better or worse," she said.

The kick went up, and forty thousand people rose to see where it would land.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: In the United States, every new employee must complete Section 1 of Form I-9, which verifies identity and permission to work, no later than their first day of paid work.
story:
Levi folded the interview shirt a second time before wearing it, because the first fold had left a crease like a scar across the chest, and he had decided that a crease could presage a bad impression the way a single grey cloud could presage a rained-out afternoon. Then he rode his bike to the Aquatics Center with the shirt flapping over his arm, changed in the family bathroom, and stood at the front desk trying to look like someone who had saved lives before, when in truth his greatest rescue to date involved a cricket in the shower.

"You're the new guard?" said the woman at the desk, whose laminated name tag read MS. PELLETIER. "Orientation's in the back room. Go on, you're the last one."

The back room smelled of chlorine and old coffee, and there were four other teenagers already seated, including Ali, who had beaten Levi to the job by a week and now wore a staff shirt with the smugness of a retired general. "Behold," Ali said, "the rookie." Levi sat down next to him and stole a pen from the middle of the table as a form of revenge.

Ms. Pelletier passed out clipboards, one to each of them, and Levi found himself holding a form he had never seen before, dense with small print and numbered boxes. "Before you get in the water," she said, "everybody takes care of this. It's Form I-9, and you complete Section 1, no exceptions." She tapped her own clipboard. "Section 1 has to be done no later than your first day of paid work, so that means today, since your first paid shift starts in an hour."

Levi read the top of the page carefully, partly because he wanted to get it right and partly because Ali was leaning over pretending to check his answers, which was annoying in a way Levi found almost comfortable. The form asked for his address, his date of birth, and then a section on citizenship, where he had to check a box attesting that he was a citizen or national of the United States. His hand hovered. It seemed like a strange thing to be asked by a pool. He checked the box, printed his name, dated it, and only then noticed the small line reminding him that Section 1 was to be completed no later than the first day of paid work, which meant that this form, this dry bureaucratic document, was technically the last thing standing between him and being paid to sit in a chair and blow a whistle.

"Did you know," Levi whispered to Ali, "that in the whole United States, every new employee has to do this? Not just lifeguards. Every single one."

"I did know," Ali said. "I did mine last week, which makes me your senior."

"You've been senior for six days."

"Seniority is seniority," Ali said, and stole the pen back.

Ms. Pelletier collected the clipboards, glanced at Levi's form, and slid it into a blue folder. "Good. For Section 2 you bring me documents, an ID and something that proves you can work, but that's my job, not yours. Now, whistle drills." She handed out whistles on lanyards, and for the next twenty minutes five teenagers stood in the shallow end practicing short blasts and long blasts, which produced a sound like a moribund carousel and caused a lap swimmer in lane four to stop and glare at them with the fury of a man whose rhythm had been ruined by teenagers.

At the end, Ms. Pelletier said his first real shift would be Saturday morning, six-thirty, the dead hour when the pool belonged to elderly lap swimmers and the light came through the big windows in long pale bars. "Don't be late," she said. "And bring your documents, because if your I-9 isn't finished properly, you can't work." She said it lightly, but Levi heard the firmness underneath, the way a joke about the water being cold still meant the water was cold.

That night he texted Ali: Do you actually know where your social security card is. Ali texted back a photo of a drawer labelled IMPORTANT STUFF containing what appeared to be a single battery and a broken pair of sunglasses, followed by the message "my mom is handling it. she says and I quote, an adage of the household: nothing important is ever where you looked first." Levi went to find his own card, and it was, in fact, not where he had looked first, or second, but in the third place, a canvas pouch in the kitchen drawer with the takeout menus, as if the United States government and the local Thai restaurant were colleagues. He put the card in his interview shirt's chest pocket, folded the shirt once along the old crease, and set it on his desk beside the whistle, so that the whole arrangement, card and whistle and shirt, sat there in the lamplight looking exactly like the first day of something.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: MLA style cites sources in the text with the author's name and page number in parentheses, and lists the full sources at the end under the heading 'Works Cited'.
story:
Ms. Qureshi had taped a sign to the library door that said Writing Club, 3:15, Bring Snacks, and someone had crossed out Snacks and written Opinions. Mia arrived with both: a bag of pretzels and a five-page paper she had written for her history class, returned that morning with a red circle around the final page and a single comment in the margin. Fix this heading. She had written "Works Cited," same as she had done all year in English, and Mr. Hendricks, who taught history like it was a courtroom, had not appreciated it.

Cora was already at the corner table, eating sunflower seeds and shelling them onto a napkin with the concentration of a jeweler. "Let me see the carnage," she said, and Mia handed the paper over. Laura leaned across, chewing the cap of her pen.

"He circled it twice," Cora said. "That's deliberate. That's a man who wants you to feel the circle."

"He wants a bibliography," Mia said. "But in English, Ms. Qureshi has us put the author's name and page number right in the parentheses in the text, and then the full sources at the end under a heading that says 'Works Cited.' I've done it that way since September. It's muscle memory now. My hands type it before I've decided anything." She took a pretzel and didn't eat it. "And the worst part is he never said what a bibliography is instead. He just circled."

Ms. Qureshi came over with her mug, which said World's Adequate Teacher, a gift, Mia suspected, from a former student with a sense of humor. She looked at the circled heading for a long moment, the way a doctor looks at an X-ray before saying anything worth hearing.

"What I always tell students," Ms. Qureshi said, "is that conventions are agreements, not laws of physics. Nobody's going to impugn your character over a heading. But conventions tell your reader what to expect, and if you break the agreement, the reader stops trusting the rest." She tapped the parentheses in Mia's second paragraph, the little (Ashworth 44) sitting there like a stamped passport. "In here you cite in the text, author and page, and the full list goes at the end under 'Works Cited.' That's the English department's agreement. Mr. Hendricks has a different one. You're not wrong. You're just in the wrong country."

"That's a lugubrious way to describe a Tuesday," Cora said, and Laura snorted so hard her pen cap flew off and rolled under the radiator.

Mia spread the paper flat and looked at her own argument, the one she had built about why the town had rerouted the river road in 1961, with two sources from the county archive and one from a newspaper database. She had been proud of the reasoning: the road wasn't moved for flood control, whatever the official report claimed, but because the cannery owner wanted the truck route past his loading dock. The archival letters made that clear, or clear enough. Mr. Hendricks had written "plausible" in the margin, which from him was practically a parade, and Mia had begun to suspect that "plausible" was the ceiling of certainty in history, that the etiology of anything, the true why of it, was always going to be partly under the radiator somewhere, unreachable.

"Here's my problem," she said slowly, turning the paper so the others could see. "The English way and the history way aren't really different opinions. They're different courtesies. English readers want to know right where the evidence is. History readers apparently want the whole map at the back. But the evidence is the same either way. So I don't actually need to change my argument, just my manners." She pulled out a clean sheet and wrote "Bibliography" at the top, then looked at it, then wrote underneath, in small letters, "(and in-text citations, author and page, per MLA, for the English version, if anyone asks)."

Laura peered at the small print. "You're keeping both?"

"I'm keeping the record of both. That feels more honest than picking one and pretending the other doesn't exist."

Ms. Qureshi smiled into her mug and said nothing, which Mia was learning was how teachers congratulated you when they wanted you to think it was your own idea. Cora swept her shells into the napkin and folded it like a burrito. Then she paused, looked at the history paper again, and frowned.

"Wait," Cora said. "This letter you cite. The one from the cannery owner. Page twelve of the archive folder?" She turned the paper toward the window light. "My mother processes that archive. She brought a box of it home last month, and I read half of it out of boredom. There's another letter in that folder. From the county engineer. Saying the flood maps were wrong and the road had to move, and the cannery thing was a coincidence." Cora shrugged, shell dust on her sleeve. "I didn't know you were writing about that or I'd have said something."

The library was quiet except for the heater ticking. Mia looked at her circled heading, then at the clean sheet, then at Cora.

"Is the box still at your house?" Mia asked.

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: Home equity is the home's current value minus what is still owed on the mortgage.
story:
The bank smelled like carpet cleaner and cold air, and Juliette stood in line behind her grandmother, holding the old woman's coat because the coat was too warm for indoors and her grandmother refused to carry anything she could make someone else carry. On the counter by the pamphlets there was a bowl of lollipops that had clearly been there since Juliette was seven, and next to it a display about mortgages that she read twice out of boredom, learning only that the bank wanted her to want one.

She was eighteen as of March, and she had a problem with a number in it: eight hundred and fifty dollars, the security deposit on the apartment she wanted to share with Hala starting in September, plus first month's rent, plus the fact that her savings account currently held four hundred and twelve dollars earned over two summers of scooping ice cream. Hala had texted her a floor plan with the words "our kitchen!!!" and three exclamation points, and Juliette had stared at it in the dark of her bedroom feeling something nascent and hard to name, half thrill, half vertigo, the sensation of a life that was hers to ruin or keep.

Her grandmother was at the bank to sign papers about selling her house. This had become the whole family's business in the past month, though the house belonged to no one but her. Grandpa had fixed the porch steps the summer before he died, and now a young couple from the city was buying the place, and the paperwork had apparently multiplied like wet bread.

At the next teller window stood Mr. Kovalenko from two doors down, the man whose dog had once commandeered Juliette's entire lunch on the front lawn, an animal with no concept of private property. He was selling too. Juliette gathered this from the way the two conversations leaned toward each other, hers and her grandmother's, like plants toward the same window. Mr. Kovalenko's house was smaller, but he'd bought it late, after the divorce, and he still owed on it. Her grandmother had paid hers off the year Juliette started kindergarten; she remembered the party, remembered eating cake on those porch steps, though she had not known then what was being celebrated.

"That's a big number," Mr. Kovalenko said to his teller, a young guy whose name tag said LYAM, and Juliette realized with a small jolt that Lyam had been in her grade's advanced math until he switched to the vocational track junior year. He was nodding at whatever figure was on his screen with the professional calm of someone being trusted for the first time.

"How much are you walking away with?" Mr. Kovalenko asked her grandmother, in the too-loud voice of a man who talks across rooms as a matter of policy.

"Enough to be dangerous," her grandmother said, which was not an answer, and everyone in line laughed, and then, because she was incapable of leaving it there, she added, "It helps that I own all of it. Home equity is the home's current value minus what is still owed on the mortgage. I owe nothing. You still owe plenty."

"That's chicanery," Mr. Kovalenko said cheerfully, pointing at her, "the way you put that."

"It's arithmetic," her grandmother said. "Same house, more or less, different money. That's the whole joke."

Juliette stood there doing the math without meaning to. The houses on that street sold in the same range; she'd looked it up once out of curiosity, back when the family was arguing. Mr. Kovalenko's would go for about what her grandmother's would. But his sale money had to go back to whoever held his mortgage, whatever was still owed, and only what remained was his to carry away. Her grandmother owed nothing, so the whole sale price came to her, minus fees, minus the realtor, minus whatever taxes the pamphlets probably explained. Same street, same market, wildly different endings. It was almost unfair, except that her grandmother had spent thirty years paying it down, month by month, on a school librarian's salary, while Mr. Kovalenko had started fifteen years ago with a divorce and a loan. Juliette found she couldn't decide whether the difference was discipline or luck, or whether those were even different things by the time you were seventy.

The teller called them forward. Her grandmother signed with the little pen on the chain, and Juliette watched the pen fight her the way chained pens fight everyone, which was possibly the only genuinely fair experience available in a bank. Then it was Juliette's turn, and Lyam looked up and said, "Hey, aren't you the one who set off the chem lab sprinkler?" and she said, "That was Hala, and it was one flame, and I supervised," and he laughed and opened a savings account for her in four minutes, during which he explained deposits, real ones: you hand over the money, the bank holds it, it earns a sliver of interest while it sits there doing nothing, which was the closest thing to rest money ever got.

"The apartment people will want proof of funds," Lyam said, sliding her a printed slip. "First month, deposit. Landlords love a deposit, it's their favorite thing, they hold it hostage until you leave the place better than cavemen found it."

"How much would a down payment be?" she asked. "On a place. A small one."

"On a condo around here, maybe five percent to start, more if you can. Then the mortgage is the rest, and you pay it for a very long time and slowly the equity grows." He said it lightly, the way you'd describe weather, and Juliette thought of her grandmother's cake on the porch steps, thirty years compressed into a party nobody had explained to her.

Outside, her grandmother was waiting on the wide stone steps, coat back on, sunglasses from 1989 deployed against a sun that barely deserved them. Juliette held the deposit slip in her hand, four hundred and twelve dollars officially existing somewhere, eight hundred and fifty officially due.

"You could cover the deposit," her grandmother said, apropos of nothing, watching the street. "If you needed it. From what I'm walking away with."

"I might need it," Juliette said. "I don't know yet."

"Nobody ever knows yet," her grandmother said, and put out her arm for Juliette to steady her on the top step, which they both knew she could manage alone.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Concussion guidelines say an athlete with a suspected concussion should not return to play on the same day, even if they feel fine.
story:
I am not a liar by nature, whatever Darren says. Darren says a lot of things, mostly about my skating, which is fair, but the mendacity charge came from a single incident in November involving his sister's boyfriend and a rumor I may have repeated in a slightly improved form. Improved is not the same as false. That is my position and I am keeping it.

The community center rink smells like burnt coffee and disinfectant, a noxious combination that the zamboni somehow makes worse, and by the third period of our Tuesday games I have usually stopped noticing it. Not that Tuesday. Tuesday we were up two goals on Westfield with a period left, and Aedan, our best winger, went into the boards behind the net at an angle that made the whole bench go quiet. The sound was like a book dropped flat on a floor.

He got up on his own, which everyone treated as good news, and skated to the bench holding his helmet on with one hand like it might float away. "I'm fine," he said. He said it twice more before anyone asked him anything, which should have been the first clue. When Coach asked him what the score was, Aedan said four to nothing, which was wrong in our favor, so he wasn't even flattering himself.

I knew the thing about concussions because Ms. Weber made our whole junior class sit through a first aid unit in the spring, and while everyone else played cell phone hockey under the desks, I had actually read the handout, mostly because I'd been seated in the front row after the rumor incident. The guideline was plain: an athlete with a suspected concussion should not return to play the same day, even if they feel fine. The "even if they feel fine" part was underlined in the handout, which I remember thinking was unusual for a district document, since the district rarely admitted anything might go wrong.

"Same day," I said to Coach. "Not even if he feels fine. That's the rule." Aedan heard me and turned in a way that suggested my face was a thing he was thinking about punching. Coach said he'd played through worse in 1994, which is what men who peaked in 1994 say, and started writing Aedan's number on the line for the final period.

Aedan then delivered a performance I have to admire in retrospect, though at the time I excoriated him for it under my breath, which is a habit of mine, saying terrible things quietly enough that only Darren can hear them. Aedan claimed the hit was to his shoulder, not his head, which the entire bench had heard with its own ears. He claimed the score answer had been a joke. He claimed, and this was the masterstroke, that our playoff hopes were his responsibility, as though the rest of us were decorative.

Here is where I could tell you I stood up to Coach and got Aedan pulled, and for two days at school that is roughly the version I told, with minor improvements. The truth is duller and I am trying out duller lately. What actually happened: I didn't stand up. I stood beside the whiteboard where the lines are written and put my hand flat over Aedan's number so Coach couldn't put it on the ice, like a very cowardly picket line, one boy, one mitten-sized glove. Darren laughed so hard he had to leave the immediate area. Coach called me something I won't repeat and sent Aedan to the rink office, where the community center had a laminated policy sheet taped inside the cupboard door, and a tired woman with a lanyard read it out loud, including the "even if they feel fine" part, over the phone to Aedan's mother, who said, "Then why is the coach arguing with a teenager about it?"

We won anyway, four to two, both goals by the kid who replaced Aedan, which is either proof of nothing or proof that Aedan's whole speech was theater. Aedan texted me that night from urgent care, where they told him he did have a concussion, mild, and that the second hit is the one that ruins you. He didn't thank me. His text said, "you're still a liar," and then, thirty seconds later, "good game though."

Saturday at the rink I was telling the improved version to a group of sophomores, the one where I confronted Coach directly, when Aedan arrived in street clothes for the game he couldn't play, still holding his helmet for no practical reason, like a man who missed his own head. He stood at the edge of the group listening, arms crossed, saying nothing. Then he picked up a puck off the boards, weighed it in his hand, and said, "Tell them the whiteboard part too, Joseph. That's the best part."

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: In a 2014 study led by David Yeager, students were more likely to revise essays when critical comments came with a note saying the teacher had high standards and believed they could meet them.
story:
Daniel pushed the peas around his plate while his father asked, again, how the robotics build was going. Fine, he said. Good, he said. The truth was that Braeden's code for the autonomous routine was a mess, tangled and slow, and Daniel had said nothing about it for two weeks because the last time he'd said anything, Braeden had stopped talking to him for three days.

"You're doing that thing," his mother said, "where you answer in one syllable and eat like you're being timed."

"I have to tell Braeden his pathing algorithm is bad," Daniel said. "Districts are in nine days. If I tell him wrong, he quits. If I don't tell him, we lose." He set down his fork. "Those are the options."

Elisha, who had been invited to stay for lasagna because his own parents were at some gala, looked up from his second helping. "There's a third option," he said. "You could tell him you believe he can fix it."

"Belief isn't code."

"Last semester I tanked the first draft of my Yeager essay," Elisha said. "My psych teacher graded it, and I was going to blow off the revision. Then she told me about the study it was based on, and I actually paid attention."

Daniel waited. His father pretended to refill the water glasses so he could keep listening.

"In a 2014 study led by David Yeager," Elisha said, "students were more likely to revise their essays when the critical comments came with a note saying the teacher had high standards and believed they could meet them. That's it. One sentence of belief stuck onto the criticism, and people picked up the pen instead of throwing it."

"That sounds too easy," Daniel's mother said.

"It's not a trick," Elisha said. "You actually have to believe it. That's the part people skip." He went back to his lasagna, and the table moved on to whether the garlic bread had been underdone, but Daniel stayed where he was.

He tried to introspect, the way his therapist had taught him, sorting what he actually felt from what he wanted to feel. He wanted Braeden's code to be better without anyone having to be uncomfortable. That was cowardice dressed up as tact. But underneath the cowardice there was something real: he did believe Braeden could rewrite the routine. Braeden had taught himself Python over one summer with a library card and a broken laptop. Daniel had watched him do it. So the belief wasn't a strategy. It was just a fact he'd been withholding, and withholding it had become a disincentive for Braeden to take any criticism seriously, because criticism from Daniel had started to sound like a verdict rather than an invitation.

"You're staring at the wall," his father said.

"I'm writing something in my head."

"Finish the lasagna first," his mother said. "The wall can wait."

He ate, but while he ate he drafted. Not the whole speech, because a speech would land like a speech, but the opening. He knew Braeden well enough to know that vague praise would read as a cushion, something soft put there so the blow would hurt less, and Braeden would resent the cushion more than the blow. It had to be judicious: precise about what was wrong, precise about what had been right, and honest in one sentence about the second thing. He wrote it on his phone under the table and deleted it twice.

After dinner he carried his plate to the sink, and instead of going upstairs he put on his jacket. "I'm walking to Braeden's," he said.

"Now? It's almost nine."

"Nine days," Daniel said. "I did the math."

His father drove him instead, idling at the curb while Daniel stood on the porch and rang the bell, and it occurred to him only then that he had not decided whether to lead with the criticism or the belief, and that whichever he chose would shape everything after. Braeden opened the door in socks, holding a controller, wary already.

"What," Braeden said.

"Can I come in for a minute?"

"My mom's in the bath."

"Then I'll talk fast." Daniel stepped inside, into the hallway that smelled like their house always smelled, like space heaters and old coffee. "The pathing algorithm is the reason we lost the scrimmage. It recalculates every loop instead of caching the obstacles, so we're burning half a second per turn, and half a second is the whole match. That's the criticism. It's specific, and it's not personal."

Braeden's jaw set. "Okay. Got it. Anything else, coach?"

"One thing." Daniel had practiced the sentence on the walk from the car, and it still came out slower than he wanted. "You taught yourself Python in one summer on that garbage laptop, and nobody on the team could have done that. Including me. I'm telling you the algorithm is bad because I think you're the only one who can make it fast." He stopped there, because the next thing he'd planned sounded like a speech.

Braeden looked at him for a long moment, then at the controller in his hand, then down the hall toward his room. "The cache idea," he said. "You want to see something?"
